import Mathlib
/-! QED-E103: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
Let N_{A4}(X) be the number of quartic number fields with Galois group A4 and |discriminant| ≤ X.
Malle predicts N_{A4}(X) ~ c X^{1/2} log X; Loughran-Paterson proved the matching lower bound.
The best upper bound is N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^{0.7784...+ε} (Bhargava-Shankar-Taniguchi-Thorne-Tsimerman-
Zhao). Lower this exponent.
Informal statement: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/ℚ with Gal(L̃/ℚ) ≅ A4 and |Δ_L| ≤ X. Prove
N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^β for some β < 0.7784 (ideally β = 1/2 + ε).
Formalization notes: Instead of isomorphism classes of fields we count subfields K of ℂ
(`IntermediateField ℚ ℂ`). An A4-quartic field has trivial automorphism group, so each
isomorphism class corresponds to exactly 4 subfields of ℂ; this changes counts by the constant
factor 4, irrelevant for the exponent. A subfield K is an A4-quartic iff [K:ℚ] = 4 and its normal
closure in ℂ has degree 12 over ℚ (A4 is the only transitive subgroup of S4 of order 12).
The discriminant is Mathlib's `NumberField.discr`; the `NumberField` instance is supplied by an
existential over the (Prop-valued) class, which holds exactly when K is finite-dimensional.
To avoid any junk value from cardinalities of possibly infinite sets, the claim bounds the size
of EVERY finite family of such fields with |Δ| ≤ X (equivalent to bounding N_{A4}(X), which is
finite by Hermite). Proving `Claim` means some exponent β < 0.7784 works for all X ≥ 1 with a
fixed constant C; `¬Claim` means no exponent below 0.7784 works (which would contradict Malle's
conjecture). Known: X^{1/2} log X ≪ N_{A4}(X) ≪ X^{0.7784...+ε}; every β strictly below 0.7784 is a
strict improvement on the record exponent 0.7784....
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE103

/-- `K ⊆ ℂ` is a quartic field with Galois group `A4` and `|disc K| ≤ X`. -/
def IsA4QuarticUpTo (X : ℝ) (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : NumberField K,
    Module.finrank ℚ K = 4 ∧
    -- the Galois closure of K (smallest normal subfield of ℂ containing K) has degree 12,
    -- which for a quartic field means Galois group A4
    (∃ M : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ, K ≤ M ∧ Normal ℚ M ∧ Module.finrank ℚ M = 12 ∧
      ∀ M' : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ, K ≤ M' → Normal ℚ M' → M ≤ M') ∧
    |((@NumberField.discr K _ h : ℤ) : ℝ)| ≤ X

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ β : ℝ, β < (0.7784 : ℝ) ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ X : ℝ, 1 ≤ X →
    ∀ S : Finset (IntermediateField ℚ ℂ), (∀ K ∈ S, IsA4QuarticUpTo X K) →
      (S.card : ℝ) ≤ C * X ^ β

end OpenProblems.QEDE103
prov_reason: Lowering the A4-quartic upper-bound exponent is the standard open target left by BSTTTZ (Thm 1.4) and cited as the record by Loughran-Paterson.

title: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
credit: Özlük–Snyder (Canad. J. Math. 58, 2006; earlier 1999 work) and Rubinstein (Duke 2001) for support (−2,2); Katz–Sarnak (1999) density conjectures.
plain: Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
math: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that $\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\!\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E104: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix
law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
Informal statement: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and
even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that
$\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to
\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.
Formalization notes:
* GRH: every zero of `DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ` (any modulus `q ≥ 1`) in `0 < Re s < 1` has `Re s = 1/2`.
  Under GRH the nontrivial zeros of `L(s, χ_{8d})` are exactly the points `1/2 + iγ` with `L = 0`, so the zero sum is
  `Σ_{γ ∈ ℝ} m(1/2 + iγ) φ(γ log X / 2π)` where `m(s)` is the order of vanishing (least `k` with
  `L^{(k)}(s) ≠ 0`, `0` at non-zeros). It is written as a `tsum` over `ℝ` (countable support; absolutely summable for
  Schwartz `φ` by the zero-counting bound `N(T, χ) ≪ T log(qT)`). The trivial zero at `s = 0` is not on the line.
* `χ_{8d}` = Kronecker symbol `(8d/·)`: for odd `n` it equals the Jacobi symbol `(8d/n)`, and it vanishes at even `n`.
  For `d` odd squarefree positive this is a primitive even real character mod `8d` (8d is a fundamental
  discriminant). We do not construct it: for each `d` we sum over all Dirichlet characters mod `8d` satisfying this
  defining property (there is exactly one), using `finsum`.
* The family: `d` odd squarefree with `X < d ≤ 2X`; `|𝓕|` is its cardinality.
* Test functions: real-valued, even, smooth, with all `|x|^k |φ^{(m)}(x)|` bounded (Schwartz).
  `φ̂(ξ) = ∫ φ(x) e^{−2πixξ} dx` (hand-defined). The condition `supp φ̂ ⊂ (−σ,σ)` is encoded as `φ̂(ξ) = 0` for
  `|ξ| ≥ σ`; as `σ > 2` is existential, the two versions give equivalent claims (shrink `σ`).
* Symplectic density `W(x) = 1 − sin(2πx)/(2πx)` (junk value `1` at `x = 0`, a null set).
* Claim := GRH → ∃ σ > 2, ∀ admissible φ, one-level density → ∫ φ W as `X → ∞` (real `X`).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE104
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical
open Filter

/-- The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for all Dirichlet `L`-functions. -/
def GRH : Prop :=
  ∀ (q : ℕ) (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ (q + 1)) (s : ℂ),
    DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

/-- `χ` is the Kronecker symbol `(8d/·)` as a character mod `8d`. -/
def IsChi8d (d : ℕ) (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ (8 * d)) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, χ (n : ZMod (8 * d)) =
    if n % 2 = 1 then (((jacobiSym (8 * (d : ℤ)) n : ℤ) : ℂ)) else 0

/-- Order of vanishing of `f` at `s` (`0` if `f s ≠ 0`). -/
def ord (f : ℂ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) : ℕ := sInf {k : ℕ | iteratedDeriv k f s ≠ 0}

/-- `Σ_γ m(1/2 + iγ) φ(γ log X / 2π)` over the zeros of `L(s, χ)` on the critical line. -/
def zeroSum {N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (X : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑' γ : ℝ, (ord (DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ) ((1 / 2 : ℂ) + (γ : ℂ) * Complex.I) : ℝ) *
    φ (γ * Real.log X / (2 * Real.pi))

/-- The family `d` odd squarefree, `X < d ≤ 2X`. -/
def family (X : ℝ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (Finset.Ioc ⌊X⌋₊ ⌊2 * X⌋₊).filter (fun d : ℕ => Odd d ∧ Squarefree d)

/-- `Σ_γ φ(γ log X / 2π)` for `χ_{8d}` (summed over the unique character mod `8d` with the defining
property; `0` for the excluded value `d = 0`, which never lies in the family). -/
def chiZeroSum (d : ℕ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (X : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if h : d = 0 then 0 else
    haveI : NeZero (8 * d) := ⟨by omega⟩
    ∑ᶠ χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ (8 * d), if IsChi8d d χ then zeroSum χ φ X else 0

/-- The averaged one-level density. -/
def oneLevel (X : ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ((family X).card : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ d ∈ family X, chiZeroSum d φ X

/-- Even real Schwartz function. -/
def IsEvenSchwartz (φ : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ r : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ r φ) ∧
  (∀ k m : ℕ, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, |x| ^ k * |iteratedDeriv m φ x| ≤ C) ∧
  (∀ x : ℝ, φ (-x) = φ x)

/-- Fourier transform `φ̂(ξ) = ∫ φ(x) e^{-2πixξ} dx`. -/
def fhat (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (ξ : ℝ) : ℂ :=
  ∫ x : ℝ, Complex.exp ((((-2) * Real.pi * x * ξ : ℝ) : ℂ) * Complex.I) * (φ x : ℂ)

/-- Symplectic one-level density `1 − sin(2πx)/(2πx)`. -/
def Wsp (x : ℝ) : ℝ := 1 - Real.sin (2 * Real.pi * x) / (2 * Real.pi * x)

def Claim : Prop :=
  GRH → ∃ σ : ℝ, 2 < σ ∧ ∀ φ : ℝ → ℝ, IsEvenSchwartz φ →
    (∀ ξ : ℝ, σ ≤ |ξ| → fhat φ ξ = 0) →
      Tendsto (fun X : ℝ => oneLevel X φ) atTop (nhds (∫ x : ℝ, φ x * Wsp x))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE104
M_fix_reason: The statement is correct (symplectic density W(x) = 1 − sin(2πx)/(2πx), scaling log X/2π). The 'why' is wrong: the symplectic transition is at support 1 and is already covered; going past 2 is a character-sum barrier, not a new test of the symplectic law. Fix the rationale.
prov_reason: Extending the support of the one-level density for quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond (−2,2) is a long-standing, explicitly recognized problem in the Katz–Sarnak programme (red-team: 'long-known program').

title: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
credit: Goldston, Gonek, Özlük, Snyder (2000), 'On the pair correlation of zeros of the Riemann zeta-function', Proc. London Math. Soc.
plain: Montgomery's function F(α) is known only for |α|≤1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2−|α|−ε on 1≤|α|≤3/2, while the conjecture says F(α)=1 there. Improve this lower bound.
math: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. Prove that for some $\delta>0$ and all $\alpha\in[1,1+\delta]$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}F(\alpha,T)\ge \tfrac32-\alpha+\delta$, or prove $\liminf_T \int_{1}^{3/2}F(\alpha,T)\,d\alpha>1/8$ (the value forced by the GGOS bound).
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E105: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
Montgomery's pair-correlation function F(α) is known only for |α| ≤ 1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions,
Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2 − |α| − ε on 1 ≤ |α| ≤ 3/2, while the conjecture says F(α) = 1 there.
Improve this lower bound.
Informal statement: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet L-functions. Prove that for some δ > 0 and all α ∈ [1, 1+δ],
liminf_{T→∞} F(α,T) ≥ 3/2 − α + δ, or prove liminf_T ∫_1^{3/2} F(α,T) dα > 1/8 (the value forced by the GGOS bound).
Formalization notes: Montgomery's normalization: F(α,T) = (T/(2π) · log T)⁻¹ Σ_{0<γ,γ'≤T} T^{iα(γ−γ')} w(γ−γ'),
w(u) = 4/(4+u²), the sum over ordinates of zeros of ζ on the critical line counted with multiplicity; the sum is real
and equals the cosine form used here. Multiplicity of a zero ρ is the least k with ζ^{(k)}(ρ) ≠ 0 (`zetaOrder`;
it is 0 at non-zeros, so summing over all real γ with weight `mult` is a finite sum, written with `finsum`). Under
GRH (which includes RH via the trivial character mod 1) every nontrivial zero is of the form 1/2 + iγ, so this sum
runs over all nontrivial zeros. GRH is stated for all Dirichlet characters mod q ≥ 1 (Mathlib's `LFunction`, the
completed analytic continuation) in the open strip 0 < Re s < 1; imprimitive characters only add zeros on Re s = 0,
which are excluded. liminf statements are written with explicit ε, T₀. Claim is the implication GRH → (target 1 ∨
target 2), matching the "or" in the problem. Note: ¬Claim would require proving GRH, so only the positive direction
is realistic; this is inherent to a conditional problem.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE105

/-- The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for all Dirichlet `L`-functions. -/
def GRH : Prop :=
  ∀ (q : ℕ) (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ (q + 1)) (s : ℂ),
    DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

/-- Order of vanishing of `ζ` at `s` (`0` if `ζ s ≠ 0`). -/
noncomputable def zetaOrder (s : ℂ) : ℕ := sInf {k : ℕ | iteratedDeriv k riemannZeta s ≠ 0}

/-- Multiplicity of `1/2 + iγ` as a zero of `ζ`, restricted to `0 < γ ≤ T`. -/
noncomputable def mult (T γ : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  if 0 < γ ∧ γ ≤ T then (zetaOrder ((1 / 2 : ℂ) + (γ : ℂ) * Complex.I) : ℝ) else 0

/-- Montgomery's weight. -/
noncomputable def w (u : ℝ) : ℝ := 4 / (4 + u ^ 2)

/-- Montgomery's pair-correlation function `F(α, T)`. -/
noncomputable def F (α T : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (T / (2 * Real.pi) * Real.log T)⁻¹ *
    ∑ᶠ γ : ℝ, ∑ᶠ γ' : ℝ,
      mult T γ * mult T γ' * Real.cos (α * (γ - γ') * Real.log T) * w (γ - γ')

def Claim : Prop :=
  GRH →
    ((∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ α ∈ Set.Icc (1 : ℝ) (1 + δ), ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
        ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T : ℝ, T₀ ≤ T → 3 / 2 - α + δ - ε ≤ F α T) ∨
     (∃ c : ℝ, 1 / 8 < c ∧ ∃ T₀ : ℝ, ∀ T : ℝ, T₀ ≤ T →
        c ≤ intervalIntegral (fun α : ℝ => F α T) 1 (3 / 2) MeasureTheory.volume))

end OpenProblems.QEDE105
prov_reason: Asks for a strict improvement of the Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder GRH lower bound for F(α) on [1, 3/2]; the refs do not pose this improvement explicitly.

title: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
credit: Cohen, Lenstra, 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', LNM 1068 (1984); Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for the first moment
plain: Davenport–Heilbronn showed the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields is 2, as Cohen–Lenstra predicts. Cohen–Lenstra also predict the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6. Prove this, or at least that the average is bounded.
math: Let $K$ range over imaginary quadratic fields with $|D_K|<X$. Cohen–Lenstra ($\mathbb E\,\#\mathrm{Sur}(\mathrm{Cl}_K,H)=1$ for $H=(\mathbb Z/3)^2$) predict $\frac{1}{\#\{K\}}\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\to 6$. Prove this limit, or prove $\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\ll X$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E106: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
Davenport-Heilbronn showed that the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields K is 2,
as Cohen-Lenstra predict. Cohen-Lenstra also predict that the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6.
Prove this.
Informal statement: Let K range over imaginary quadratic fields with |D_K| < X. Cohen-Lenstra
(E #Sur(Cl_K, H) = 1 for H = (ℤ/3)²) predict (1/#{K}) Σ_K |Cl_K[3]|² → 6 as X → ∞. Prove this
limit. (Fallback, not formalized here: Σ_K |Cl_K[3]|² ≪ X.)
Formalization notes: Imaginary quadratic fields are represented by subfields K of ℂ
(`IntermediateField ℚ ℂ`) of degree 2 over ℚ that are not contained in ℝ. Each imaginary
quadratic field has exactly one image in ℂ (quadratic fields are normal), so this counts
isomorphism classes exactly once. The discriminant is `NumberField.discr`, with the
(Prop-valued) `NumberField` instance supplied existentially; it exists exactly for
finite-dimensional K. `tors3 K` is the number of elements c of the class group of the ring of
integers with c³ = 1, i.e. |Cl_K[3]| (the class group is finite, so `Nat.card` is faithful).
`fieldsUpTo X` is finite for each X (Hermite), so `Set.ncard` and `finsum` are faithful; for
small X the average is 0/0 = 0 in Lean, which does not affect the limit. Proving `Claim` proves
the Cohen-Lenstra second-moment prediction (average → 6); proving `¬Claim` disproves it.
Identity behind 6: |Cl[3]|² = #Hom(Cl, (ℤ/3)²) = Σ_{H ≤ (ℤ/3)²} #Sur(Cl, H), with 1 + 4 + 1 subgroups.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE106

/-- `K ⊆ ℂ` is an imaginary quadratic field with `|disc K| < X`. -/
def IsImagQuadUpTo (X : ℝ) (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : NumberField K,
    Module.finrank ℚ K = 2 ∧
    (∃ x : K, (x : ℂ).im ≠ 0) ∧
    |((@NumberField.discr K _ h : ℤ) : ℝ)| < X

/-- The (finite) set of imaginary quadratic subfields of `ℂ` with `|disc| < X`. -/
def fieldsUpTo (X : ℝ) : Set (IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) :=
  {K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ | IsImagQuadUpTo X K}

/-- `|Cl_K[3]|`: the number of ideal classes of `𝓞_K` whose cube is trivial. -/
noncomputable def tors3 (K : IntermediateField ℚ ℂ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {c : ClassGroup (NumberField.RingOfIntegers K) // c ^ 3 = 1}

/-- Average of `|Cl_K[3]|²` over imaginary quadratic fields with `|disc| < X`. -/
noncomputable def secondMoment (X : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ᶠ K ∈ fieldsUpTo X, ((tors3 K : ℝ) ^ 2)) / ((fieldsUpTo X).ncard : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  Filter.Tendsto secondMoment Filter.atTop (nhds (6 : ℝ))

end OpenProblems.QEDE106
prov_reason: The average 6 for |Cl[3]|² over imaginary quadratic fields is a direct Cohen-Lenstra prediction and a well-known open case beyond Davenport-Heilbronn.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
plain: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
math: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E107: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
Jörgens proved that a convex entire solution of det D^2 u = 1 in the plane is a quadratic
polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 and ask whether entire
solutions on the elliptic branch are still quadratic.
Informal statement: Let u ∈ C^4(R^2) satisfy u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 = 1, u_xx > 0 and 2 u_xy^2 < 1
on R^2. Prove or disprove that u is a quadratic polynomial.
Formalization notes: u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ with `ContDiff ℝ 4 u`. Second partials are values of the
second Fréchet derivative: u_xx = D^2u(p)(e1,e1), u_xy = D^2u(p)(e1,e2), u_yy = D^2u(p)(e2,e2)
with e1 = (1,0), e2 = (0,1). The conditions u_xx > 0 and 2u_xy^2 < 1 are exactly ellipticity of
the linearized operator; they imply convexity. "Quadratic polynomial" means
u(x,y) = a x^2 + b xy + c y^2 + d x + e y + f for real constants (any degree <= 2 polynomial).
Quadratic solutions exist (e.g. (x^2+y^2)/2), so the hypothesis is not vacuous. Proving Claim
is the Jörgens-type rigidity theorem; proving ¬Claim exhibits a non-quadratic entire elliptic
solution.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE107

/-- Second Fréchet derivative of `u` at `p` applied to `(v, w)`. -/
noncomputable def secondPartial (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) (v w : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ u) p v w

/-- Unit vector in the x direction. -/
def ex : ℝ × ℝ := (1, 0)

/-- Unit vector in the y direction. -/
def ey : ℝ × ℝ := (0, 1)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 4 u →
    (∀ p : ℝ × ℝ,
      secondPartial u p ex ex * secondPartial u p ey ey + secondPartial u p ex ey ^ 2 = 1 ∧
      0 < secondPartial u p ex ex ∧
      2 * secondPartial u p ex ey ^ 2 < 1) →
    ∃ a b c d e f : ℝ, ∀ x y : ℝ,
      u (x, y) = a * x ^ 2 + b * x * y + c * y ^ 2 + d * x + e * y + f

end OpenProblems.QEDE107
prov_reason: Notes report no literature on the permanent equation u_xx u_yy + u_xy^2 = 1; the Jörgens-type question for it was formulated by QED.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
plain: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
math: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E108: KdV with a cosine coefficient
Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy
and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy is indefinite. Can
smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
Informal statement: Consider u_t + u_xxx + (cos(x) u³)_x = 0 on 𝕋 = ℝ/2πℤ with real
u₀ ∈ C^∞(𝕋). It is Hamiltonian with H = ∫(½u_x² − ¼cos(x)u⁴), conserves ∫u and H, and
d/dt ∫u² = ½∫ sin(x) u⁴. Decide whether every such u₀ yields a global smooth solution, or
whether ‖u(t)‖_{H¹} → ∞ in finite time for some u₀.
Formalization notes:
* Functions on 𝕋 are 2π-periodic functions on ℝ. A global smooth solution is
  u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ (time, space), C^n for every n ∈ ℕ (i.e. C^∞; written this way to avoid
  `⊤` meaning analytic), 2π-periodic in x, with u(0,x) = u₀(x) and the equation holding
  pointwise for all t ≥ 0. Requiring u to be smooth on all of ℝ × ℝ (with the equation only
  for t ≥ 0) loses nothing: a C^∞ function on [0,∞) × 𝕋 extends smoothly to t < 0.
* Derivatives are partial derivatives via `deriv` of sections; `iteratedDeriv 3` for u_xxx.
* Proving `Claim`: every smooth periodic u₀ has a global smooth solution (global regularity).
  Proving `¬Claim`: some smooth u₀ has no global smooth solution; by standard local
  well-posedness in H^s (s large) with the blow-up alternative and persistence of regularity,
  this is equivalent to finite-time blow-up of ‖u(t)‖_{H¹} (the H¹ norm controls all higher
  norms for this equation), matching the dichotomy in the informal statement.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE108

/-- `u` is a global (forward in time) smooth 2π-periodic solution of
`u_t + u_xxx + (cos x · u³)_x = 0` with initial data `u₀`. -/
def IsGlobalSmoothSolution (u₀ : ℝ → ℝ) (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n u) ∧
  (∀ t x : ℝ, u (t, x + 2 * Real.pi) = u (t, x)) ∧
  (∀ x : ℝ, u (0, x) = u₀ x) ∧
  ∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → ∀ x : ℝ,
    deriv (fun s : ℝ => u (s, x)) t
      + iteratedDeriv 3 (fun y : ℝ => u (t, y)) x
      + deriv (fun y : ℝ => Real.cos y * (u (t, y)) ^ 3) x = 0

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ u₀ : ℝ → ℝ, (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n u₀) → Function.Periodic u₀ (2 * Real.pi) →
    ∃ u : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ, IsGlobalSmoothSolution u₀ u

end OpenProblems.QEDE108
M_fix_reason: Conservation laws and the L² identity check out (d/dt∫u² = ½∫ sin x u⁴). Well posed; the dichotomy is exhaustive given local well-posedness with H¹ blow-up alternative.
prov_reason: A specific inhomogeneous mKdV model chosen by QED; the literature check was incomplete (search budget ran out), but no source posing this equation was identified.

title: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
plain: Gidas-Spruck: -Delta u = u^p has no positive solution on R^n for subcritical p. Replace u^p by the value of u^p at a shifted point x+e. Is there still no positive solution, for every subcritical p?
math: Let $n\ge3$, $1<p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$, $e\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Prove or disprove: there is no positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^p$ for all $x$. (For $1<p<\frac n{n-2}$ the standard Mitidieri–Pohozaev test-function argument applies, since the shift is negligible at large scales; the open range is $\frac n{n-2}\le p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$. One may also ask whether positive solutions exist for $p\ge\frac{n+2}{n-2}$.)
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E109: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
Gidas-Spruck: -Δu = u^p has no positive entire solution on R^n for 1 < p < (n+2)/(n-2). If the
nonlinearity is evaluated at a shifted point, -Δu(x) = u(x+e)^p with e ≠ 0, is there still no
positive solution for every subcritical p?
Informal statement: Let n >= 3, 1 < p < (n+2)/(n-2), e ∈ R^n \ {0}. Prove or disprove: there is no
positive u ∈ C^2(R^n) with -Δu(x) = u(x+e)^p for all x.
Formalization notes: R^n is `Fin n → ℝ`; the Laplacian is defined from the second Fréchet
derivative as Σ_i D^2u(x)(e_i, e_i) with e_i = `Pi.single i 1` (independent of the norm used).
u(x+e)^p is the real power `Real.rpow` (u > 0, so no junk values). Claim asserts nonexistence for
all n >= 3, all subcritical p > 1 and all e ≠ 0 simultaneously; ¬Claim means a positive C^2
solution exists for some such (n, p, e). The range 1 < p < n/(n-2) is believed to follow from
the Mitidieri-Pohozaev test-function method; the open range is n/(n-2) <= p < (n+2)/(n-2). The
supercritical question p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is not part of Claim.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE109

/-- The Laplacian of `u : ℝ^n → ℝ` at `x`, via the second Fréchet derivative. -/
noncomputable def laplacian {n : ℕ} (u : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin n, fderiv ℝ (fderiv ℝ u) x (Pi.single i (1 : ℝ)) (Pi.single i (1 : ℝ))

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, 3 ≤ n → ∀ p : ℝ, 1 < p → p < ((n : ℝ) + 2) / ((n : ℝ) - 2) →
    ∀ e : Fin n → ℝ, e ≠ 0 →
      ¬ ∃ u : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ, ContDiff ℝ 2 u ∧ (∀ x, 0 < u x) ∧
        ∀ x, -(laplacian u x) = (u (x + e)) ^ p

end OpenProblems.QEDE109
prov_reason: Notes report no literature on shifted-argument Lane-Emden equations after two searches; the question is a new nonlocal variant formulated by QED.

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
credit: B. Dodson, global well-posedness and scattering for the defocusing L^2-critical NLS in d=2 (Duke Math. J. 2016)
results: Both trivial cases check out. For alpha=2pi/k, C_alpha=R^2/Z_k: the Friedrichs modes e^{ikmθ} with Bessel order k|m| match the Z_k-invariant plane functions, and Dodson applies for any mass, with mass scaled by k. For radial data the m=0 mode on the cone is the 2D radial Laplacian. The sign convention iu_t+Δu=+|u|^2u is defocusing.
plain: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
math: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E110: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrödinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
Informal statement: For α > 0 let C_α = (0,∞) × (ℝ/αℤ) with metric dr² + r²dθ² and Δ the Friedrichs
extension of the Laplacian on C_c^∞(C_α). Prove that for every α > 0 and every u₀ ∈ L²(C_α) the
solution of iu_t + Δu = |u|²u, u(0) = u₀, is global with ‖u‖_{L⁴_{t,x}(ℝ × C_α)} < ∞, hence scatters in L².
(Known: α = 2π/k, and radial data for any α.)
Formalization notes: Polar model. A point of C_α is (r, θ) ∈ (0,∞) × [0,α) (`Rg α`; [0,α) is a
fundamental domain of ℝ/αℤ), with area measure r dr dθ, so L²(C_α) pairings are
`cip α u v = ∫_{Rg α} conj(u) v r`. Spectral resolution of the Friedrichs Laplacian (Cheeger; Ford):
L²(C_α) = ⊕_{m∈ℤ} L²((0,∞), r dr) · e^{2πimθ/α}; on the m-th mode Δ = ∂_r² + r⁻¹∂_r − ν²/r² with
ν = ν_m = 2π|m|/α, and the Friedrichs extension (which selects the regular solution at r = 0; for ν ≥ 1
it is the only self-adjoint extension) is diagonalised by the Hankel transform
H_ν g(ρ) = ∫_0^∞ J_ν(ρr) g(r) r dr (unitary and self-inverse on L²(r dr)), with Δ ↦ −ρ². Hence on the
dense class D₀ of finite mode sums φ = Σ_{m∈F} f_m(r) e^{2πimθ/α} with f_m ∈ C_c^∞((0,∞)) (`testFn`),
e^{isΔ}φ = Σ_m e^{2πimθ/α} ∫_0^∞ J_ν(rρ) e^{−isρ²} H_ν f_m(ρ) ρ dρ (`flow`); here H_ν f_m is rapidly
decreasing (H_ν(L_ν f) = −ρ² H_ν f with L_ν f ∈ C_c^∞(0,∞)) and |J_ν| ≤ 1, so all integrals converge
absolutely. J_ν is defined by its power series (`besselJ`, using `Real.Gamma`). The solution concept is
the standard L²-critical one: u ∈ C(ℝ; L²(C_α)) ∩ L⁴_{t,x}(ℝ × C_α) satisfying the Duhamel formula
u(t) = e^{itΔ}u₀ − i ∫_0^t e^{i(t−τ)Δ}(|u|²u)(τ) dτ (from u_t = iΔu − i|u|²u). Since e^{isΔ} is unitary
with adjoint e^{−isΔ}, Duhamel is imposed weakly by pairing with every φ ∈ D₀:
⟨φ, u(t)⟩ = ⟨e^{−itΔ}φ, u₀⟩ − i ∫_0^t ⟨e^{i(τ−t)Δ}φ, |u|²u(τ)⟩ dτ; D₀ is dense in L², so this determines
u(t), and conversely it is equivalent to the strong Duhamel formula. The space-time integrand is
required to be integrable on [0,t] × C_α (true for genuine solutions by Hölder: e^{isΔ}φ ∈ L⁴_{t,x} by
Strichartz, |u|²u ∈ L^{4/3}_{t,x}) so the pairing is not a junk value. Global finiteness of
∫_ℝ∫ |u|⁴ r dr dθ dt is part of the solution notion; with uniqueness of such solutions (standard, via
Strichartz on cones) this is exactly "global with finite L⁴ norm" (scattering then follows by the usual
argument). `Claim`: for every α > 0 and every u₀ ∈ L²(C_α) such a solution exists. ¬Claim means some
angle α and datum u₀ for which no global finite-L⁴ solution exists (finite-time blow-up of the L⁴
norm or infinite global L⁴ norm). Functions are only used on `Rg α`; values elsewhere are irrelevant.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE110
noncomputable section

open MeasureTheory Filter Topology

/-- Polar fundamental domain of the cone `C_α`: `r > 0`, `θ ∈ [0, α)`. Points are `(r, θ)`. -/
def Rg (α : ℝ) : Set (ℝ × ℝ) := Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ) ×ˢ Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) α

/-- `L²(C_α)` inner product with the area element `r dr dθ`, conjugate-linear in the first slot. -/
def cip (α : ℝ) (u v : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) : ℂ :=
  ∫ p in Rg α, (starRingEnd ℂ) (u p) * v p * (p.1 : ℂ)

/-- `∫_{C_α} |u|²` restricted to `Rg α`, as a real number. -/
def cnormSq (α : ℝ) (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) : ℝ := ∫ p in Rg α, ‖u p‖ ^ 2 * p.1

/-- `u ∈ L²(C_α)`. -/
def IsL2 (α : ℝ) (u : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  AEStronglyMeasurable u (volume.restrict (Rg α)) ∧
    Integrable (fun p : ℝ × ℝ => ‖u p‖ ^ 2 * p.1) (volume.restrict (Rg α))

/-- Bessel function of the first kind `J_ν(x)` (`ν ≥ 0`, `x ≥ 0`) by its power series. -/
def besselJ (ν x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑' k : ℕ, (-1 : ℝ) ^ k / ((k.factorial : ℝ) * Real.Gamma ((k : ℝ) + ν + 1)) *
    (x / 2) ^ (2 * (k : ℝ) + ν)

/-- Bessel order of the angular mode `m`: `ν_m = 2π|m|/α`. -/
def order (α : ℝ) (m : ℤ) : ℝ := 2 * Real.pi * |(m : ℝ)| / α

/-- Angular mode `e^{2πimθ/α}`. -/
def angular (α : ℝ) (m : ℤ) (θ : ℝ) : ℂ :=
  Complex.exp (2 * (Real.pi : ℂ) * Complex.I * (m : ℂ) * (θ : ℂ) / (α : ℂ))

/-- Hankel transform of order `ν`: `H_ν g(ρ) = ∫_0^∞ J_ν(ρ r) g(r) r dr`. -/
def hankel (ν : ℝ) (g : ℝ → ℂ) (ρ : ℝ) : ℂ :=
  ∫ r in Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ), (besselJ ν (ρ * r) : ℂ) * g r * (r : ℂ)

/-- Radial profiles of test functions: `C^∞` with compact support in `(0, ∞)`. -/
def IsProfile (g : ℝ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ k : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ k g) ∧ ∃ a b : ℝ, 0 < a ∧ a < b ∧ ∀ r : ℝ, (r < a ∨ b < r) → g r = 0

/-- Test function `φ(r, θ) = Σ_{m ∈ F} f_m(r) e^{2πimθ/α}` (the dense class `D₀`). -/
def testFn (α : ℝ) (F : Finset ℤ) (f : ℤ → ℝ → ℂ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℂ :=
  ∑ m ∈ F, f m p.1 * angular α m p.2

/-- `e^{isΔ} φ` for `φ = testFn α F f`, via the Hankel transform on each angular mode. -/
def flow (α : ℝ) (F : Finset ℤ) (f : ℤ → ℝ → ℂ) (s : ℝ) (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℂ :=
  ∑ m ∈ F, angular α m p.2 *
    ∫ ρ in Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ), (besselJ (order α m) (p.1 * ρ) : ℂ) *
      Complex.exp (-(Complex.I * (s : ℂ) * ((ρ ^ 2 : ℝ) : ℂ))) * hankel (order α m) (f m) ρ * (ρ : ℂ)

/-- The defocusing cubic nonlinearity `|v|² v`. -/
def cubic (v : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ := fun p => ((‖v p‖ ^ 2 : ℝ) : ℂ) * v p

/-- `u` is a global solution of `i u_t + Δu = |u|²u`, `u(0) = u₀`, in `C(ℝ; L²) ∩ L⁴_{t,x}(ℝ × C_α)`,
satisfying the Duhamel formula weakly against the dense class `D₀`. -/
def GlobalScatteringSol (α : ℝ) (u0 : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) (u : ℝ → ℝ × ℝ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ t : ℝ, IsL2 α (u t)) ∧
  (∀ t₀ : ℝ, Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => cnormSq α (u t - u t₀)) (𝓝 t₀) (𝓝 0)) ∧
  Integrable (fun q : ℝ × (ℝ × ℝ) => ‖u q.1 q.2‖ ^ 4 * q.2.1)
    (volume.restrict (Set.univ ×ˢ Rg α)) ∧
  ∀ (F : Finset ℤ) (f : ℤ → ℝ → ℂ), (∀ m : ℤ, IsProfile (f m)) → ∀ t : ℝ,
    IntegrableOn (fun q : ℝ × (ℝ × ℝ) =>
        (starRingEnd ℂ) (flow α F f (q.1 - t) q.2) * cubic (u q.1) q.2 * (q.2.1 : ℂ))
      (Set.uIcc 0 t ×ˢ Rg α) ∧
    cip α (testFn α F f) (u t) =
      cip α (flow α F f (-t)) u0 -
        Complex.I * ∫ τ in (0 : ℝ)..t, cip α (flow α F f (τ - t)) (cubic (u τ))

/-- Global well-posedness with finite `L⁴_{t,x}` norm (hence scattering) for the defocusing
mass-critical NLS on every flat cone, for all `L²` data. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ α : ℝ, 0 < α → ∀ u0 : ℝ × ℝ → ℂ, IsL2 α u0 →
    ∃ u : ℝ → ℝ × ℝ → ℂ, GlobalScatteringSol α u0 u

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE110
prov_reason: This extends Dodson's mass-critical scattering theorem on R^2 to flat cones of arbitrary angle; the searches found no source that poses it.

title: Quintic Szego growth
credit: Gérard–Grellier (cubic Szegő equation, turbulent solutions); Thirouin, quadratic Szegő equation (arXiv:1710.01512).
plain: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
math: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E111: Quintic Szego growth
The cubic Szegő equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gérard–Grellier showed that
its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic
Szegő equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high
Sobolev norms.
Informal statement: On L²_+(𝕋) = {u ∈ L² : û(k) = 0 ∀ k < 0} with Szegő projector Π, consider
i∂ₜu = Π(|u|⁴u), which is globally well posed in H^s_+, s > 1/2, with conserved ‖u‖_{L²}, (Du,u) and
‖u‖_{L⁶}. Decide whether there exist u₀ ∈ C^∞(𝕋) ∩ L²_+ and s > 1/2 with
limsup_{t→∞} ‖u(t)‖_{H^s} = ∞. (`Claim`: such u₀ and s exist, and the solution is global.)
Formalization notes:
* 𝕋 = ℝ/2πℤ; functions on 𝕋 are 2π-periodic functions ℝ → ℂ. Fourier coefficients are
  û(k) = (1/2π) ∫₀^{2π} u(x) e^{−ikx} dx (`coef`).
* A global smooth solution is u : ℝ → ℝ → ℂ (time, space), C^n for every n jointly in (t,x)
  (values for t < 0 are irrelevant: a smooth function on [0,∞) × 𝕋 extends smoothly), 2π-periodic
  in x and with û(t,k) = 0 for k < 0 for all t ≥ 0, u(0) = u₀, and the equation tested on Fourier
  modes: i (d/dt) û(t,k) = (|u|⁴u)^(t,k) for all k ≥ 0, t > 0. For smooth u this is equivalent
  to the pointwise equation i∂ₜu = Π(|u|⁴u): both sides are smooth periodic functions, Πw has
  Fourier coefficients ŵ(k)·1_{k≥0}, and (∂ₜu)^ = d/dt û by differentiation under the integral;
  negative modes vanish on both sides. |u|⁴u is written (normSq u)²·u.
* H^s norm: ‖u‖²_{H^s} = Σ_k (1+k²)^s |û(k)|² (`tsum`; for smooth u(t) the series is summable,
  and a non-summable junk value 0 could only make growth harder, never fake it). Since u is smooth
  on [0,∞) × 𝕋, t ↦ ‖u(t)‖_{H^s} is continuous, so unboundedness on [0,∞) ⇔ limsup_{t→∞} = ∞.
* Existential form. `Claim` asks for a global smooth solution with unbounded H^s norm. Smooth
  solutions are unique (the nonlinearity is Lipschitz on bounded sets of H^s, s > 1/2), so this is
  the statement about "the" solution; and because existence of the global solution is part of
  `Claim`, a hypothetical failure of global well-posedness (flagged by the reviewer) cannot make
  `Claim` cheaply true: finite-time blow-up would not count as unbounded growth.
* Proving `Claim` = some smooth u₀ ∈ L²_+ has a global solution with unbounded H^s norm for some
  s > 1/2. Proving `¬Claim` = every global smooth solution has bounded H^s norms for every
  s > 1/2 (given GWP: all smooth solutions have bounded Sobolev norms).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE111
noncomputable section

/-- Fourier coefficient `û(k) = (1/2π) ∫₀^{2π} u(x) e^{−ikx} dx`. -/
def coef (w : ℝ → ℂ) (k : ℤ) : ℂ :=
  (1 / (2 * Real.pi) : ℂ) *
    ∫ x in (0 : ℝ)..(2 * Real.pi), w x * Complex.exp (-(Complex.I * (k : ℂ) * (x : ℂ)))

/-- Quintic nonlinearity `|z|⁴ z`. -/
def quintic (z : ℂ) : ℂ := ((Complex.normSq z ^ 2 : ℝ) : ℂ) * z

/-- Squared `H^s` norm `Σ_k (1+k²)^s |û(k)|²`. -/
def hsNormSq (s : ℝ) (w : ℝ → ℂ) : ℝ :=
  ∑' k : ℤ, (1 + (k : ℝ) ^ 2) ^ s * Complex.normSq (coef w k)

/-- `u₀` is a smooth function in `L²_+(𝕋)`. -/
def IsSmoothHardy (u₀ : ℝ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n u₀) ∧ (∀ x : ℝ, u₀ (x + 2 * Real.pi) = u₀ x) ∧
    ∀ k : ℤ, k < 0 → coef u₀ k = 0

/-- `u` is a global smooth solution of the quintic Szegő equation with data `u₀`. -/
def IsGlobalSolution (u₀ : ℝ → ℂ) (u : ℝ → ℝ → ℂ) : Prop :=
  (∀ n : ℕ, ContDiff ℝ n (fun q : ℝ × ℝ => u q.1 q.2)) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → ∀ x : ℝ, u t (x + 2 * Real.pi) = u t x) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t → ∀ k : ℤ, k < 0 → coef (u t) k = 0) ∧
  (∀ x : ℝ, u 0 x = u₀ x) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → ∀ k : ℤ, 0 ≤ k →
    Complex.I * deriv (fun τ : ℝ => coef (u τ) k) t = coef (fun x : ℝ => quintic (u t x)) k)

/-- Some smooth Hardy datum has a global solution whose `H^s` norm (some `s > 1/2`) is unbounded. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ (u₀ : ℝ → ℂ) (s : ℝ) (u : ℝ → ℝ → ℂ), IsSmoothHardy u₀ ∧ 1 / 2 < s ∧
    IsGlobalSolution u₀ u ∧ ∀ M : ℝ, ∃ t : ℝ, 0 ≤ t ∧ M < hsNormSq s (u t)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE111
M_fix_reason: Well posed, assuming global well-posedness in H^s_+ (s > 1/2) via H^{1/2} control and a Brezis–Gallouët argument as in the cubic case; the reviewer asked for this to be double-checked. If it failed, the question would need a 'blow-up or unbounded growth' disjunction.
prov_reason: Non-integrable quintic analogue of the cubic Szegő equation, for which Gérard–Grellier proved unbounded Sobolev growth; a quick search found work on cubic and quadratic Szegő equations but no posing of the quintic case.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
credit: Extends Jones–Przytycki (Lissajous knots and billiard knots, 1998) and Koseleff–Pecker, 'Every knot is a billiard knot', arXiv:1106.5600; periodic orbits in polyhedra: Bedaride–Rao arXiv:1104.1051.
plain: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
math: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E112: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, never hitting an edge or a
corner, traces a closed polygon in space. Do infinitely many knot types occur among these
polygons (in particular, is any of them knotted)?
Informal statement: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron T ⊂ ℝ³
admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of T and its image is an embedded closed polygon.
(a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types
of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite. The Claim is (b), which implies (a).
Formalization notes: T = {x ∈ ℝ³ : ⟪x, vᵢ⟫ ≥ −1 for i = 0..3} with vertices
v₀ = (1,1,1), v₁ = (1,−1,−1), v₂ = (−1,1,−1), v₃ = (−1,−1,1); face i is {⟪x, vᵢ⟫ = −1}, with
outward normal −vᵢ. A periodic trajectory (`PeriodicOrbit`) is an N-periodic sequence of bounce
points pₖ (N ≥ 1), each in the relative interior of a face φ(k) (on that face and strictly inside
the other three half-spaces, so never on an edge or vertex), consecutive bounce points on
different faces (so the open chords lie in the interior of T, by convexity), and the reflection
law: the outgoing direction p_{k+2} − p_{k+1} is a positive multiple of the mirror image of the
incoming direction p_{k+1} − p_k in the plane of face φ(k+1), R(d) = d − (2/3)⟪d, v⟫ v. The
image is ⋃_{k<N} [pₖ, p_{k+1}]; admissible means it is a topological circle (image of a
continuous injective map from the unit circle in ℂ). This automatically discards orbits that
retrace themselves or self-intersect; orbits traversing their image twice are allowed, as in the
notes. Knot types are compared up to homeomorphisms of ℝ³ (`KnotEquiv`): for polygonal (tame)
knots this is ambient isotopy up to mirror image, and since each such class contains at most two
isotopy classes, "infinitely many knot types" and "nontrivial knot" mean the same under either
convention. The unknot is represented by a planar triangle. Proving `Claim` = exhibiting, for
every n, n admissible orbits with pairwise inequivalent images; `¬Claim` = only finitely many
knot types occur.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE112
noncomputable section

/-- Points of ℝ³. -/
abbrev R3 : Type := Fin 3 → ℝ

/-- Euclidean inner product on ℝ³. -/
def dot (x y : R3) : ℝ := ∑ i : Fin 3, x i * y i

/-- Vertices of the regular tetrahedron `T`. -/
def tetVert : Fin 4 → R3 :=
  ![![(1 : ℝ), 1, 1], ![(1 : ℝ), -1, -1], ![(-1 : ℝ), 1, -1], ![(-1 : ℝ), -1, 1]]

/-- The regular tetrahedron `T = {x | ∀ i, ⟪x, vᵢ⟫ ≥ −1}`. -/
def tetra : Set R3 := {x : R3 | ∀ i : Fin 4, -1 ≤ dot x (tetVert i)}

/-- `p` lies in the relative interior of face `i` (the face opposite vertex `i`). -/
def OnFaceInt (i : Fin 4) (p : R3) : Prop :=
  dot p (tetVert i) = -1 ∧ ∀ j : Fin 4, j ≠ i → -1 < dot p (tetVert j)

/-- Reflection of a direction vector in the plane of face `i` (normal `vᵢ`, `‖vᵢ‖² = 3`). -/
def refl (i : Fin 4) (d : R3) : R3 :=
  d - ((2 : ℝ) / 3 * dot d (tetVert i)) • tetVert i

/-- A periodic billiard trajectory in `T` avoiding edges and vertices. -/
structure PeriodicOrbit where
  N : ℕ
  hN : 0 < N
  p : ℕ → R3
  face : ℕ → Fin 4
  periodic : ∀ k, p (k + N) = p k
  on_face : ∀ k, OnFaceInt (face k) (p k)
  next_face : ∀ k, face (k + 1) ≠ face k
  reflection : ∀ k, ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
    p (k + 2) - p (k + 1) = c • refl (face (k + 1)) (p (k + 1) - p k)

/-- The image of the trajectory: the union of its chords over one period. -/
def PeriodicOrbit.image (o : PeriodicOrbit) : Set R3 :=
  ⋃ k : Fin o.N, segment ℝ (o.p (k : ℕ)) (o.p ((k : ℕ) + 1))

/-- The image is an embedded closed curve (homeomorphic to a circle). -/
def PeriodicOrbit.Admissible (o : PeriodicOrbit) : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : Metric.sphere (0 : ℂ) 1 → R3,
    Continuous γ ∧ Function.Injective γ ∧ Set.range γ = o.image

/-- Knot equivalence up to homeomorphism of ℝ³. -/
def KnotEquiv (K₁ K₂ : Set R3) : Prop :=
  ∃ h : R3 ≃ₜ R3, h '' K₁ = K₂

/-- A planar triangle, representing the unknot. -/
def unknot : Set R3 :=
  segment ℝ (0 : R3) (Pi.single 0 1) ∪ segment ℝ (Pi.single 0 1) (Pi.single 1 1) ∪
    segment ℝ (Pi.single 1 1) (0 : R3)

/-- Part (a), implied by `Claim`: some admissible orbit is knotted. (Not the Claim.) -/
def SomeKnottedOrbit : Prop :=
  ∃ o : PeriodicOrbit, o.Admissible ∧ ¬ KnotEquiv o.image unknot

/-- Part (b): infinitely many knot types occur among admissible periodic orbits. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ o : Fin n → PeriodicOrbit, (∀ i, (o i).Admissible) ∧
    ∀ i j : Fin n, i ≠ j → ¬ KnotEquiv (o i).image (o j).image

end

end OpenProblems.QEDE112
M_fix_reason: M is well posed; Lean takes (b) as the Claim since (b) implies (a). Note for reviewers: if (a) alone is wanted as a separate problem, `SomeKnottedOrbit` is provided.
prov_reason: Transfers the cube billiard-knot (Lissajous knot) question to the regular tetrahedron; searches found work on billiard knots in cubes/cylinders and periodic orbits in polyhedra/simplices but no knot-type results for the tetrahedron.

title: Does the self-avoiding-walk growth ratio converge on the square lattice?
credit: Open problem stated in Madras-Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk (1993) and Bauerschmidt, Duminil-Copin, Goodman, Slade, Lectures on Self-Avoiding Walks (2012), Sec. 1.3.
premise_risks: Well known to specialists, so novelty is modest
Could conceivably be equivalent in difficulty to proving existence of gamma
plain: Let c_n be the number of n-step walks on the square grid that start at the origin and never visit a point twice. It is classical that c_n^{1/n} tends to a constant mu (about 2.638), and Kesten proved in 1963 that the two-step ratio c_{n+2}/c_n tends to mu^2. Does the one-step ratio c_{n+1}/c_n converge (necessarily to mu)? Numerically the ratios alternate between even and odd n with a shrinking gap, but no proof exists in dimensions 2, 3 or 4.
math: Let $c_n=\#\{(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)\in(\mathbb Z^2)^{n+1}:\omega_0=0,\ \|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1,\ \omega_i\neq\omega_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $\mu=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty} c_{n+1}/c_n$ exists. (Given Kesten's theorem $c_{n+2}/c_n\to\mu^2$, this is equivalent to $c_{n+1}/c_n\to\mu$, i.e. to the even and odd subsequences of $c_{n+1}/c_n$ having the same limit.)
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E113: Does the self-avoiding-walk growth ratio converge on the square lattice?
Let c_n be the number of n-step walks on the square grid that start at the origin and never visit a point twice. It is classical that c_n^{1/n} tends to a constant mu (about 2.638), and Kesten proved in 1963 that the two-step ratio c_{n+2}/c_n tends to mu^2. Does the one-step ratio c_{n+1}/c_n converge (necessarily to mu)? Numerically the ratios alternate between even and odd n with a shrinking gap, but no proof exists in dimensions 2, 3 or 4.
Informal statement: Let $c_n=\#\{(\omega_0,\dots,\omega_n)\in(\mathbb Z^2)^{n+1}:\omega_0=0,\ \|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1,\ \omega_i\neq\omega_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $\mu=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}$. Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty} c_{n+1}/c_n$ exists. (Given Kesten's theorem $c_{n+2}/c_n\to\mu^2$, this is equivalent to $c_{n+1}/c_n\to\mu$, i.e. to the even and odd subsequences of $c_{n+1}/c_n$ having the same limit.)
Formalization notes:
* `Adj2 a b` is the nearest-neighbour relation of the square lattice: ℓ¹-distance exactly 1.
* An n-step self-avoiding walk is an injective map `ω : Fin (n+1) → ℤ × ℤ` with `ω 0 = (0,0)`
  and `Adj2 (ω i) (ω (i+1))` for `i < n`. Every such walk stays in the box `[-n,n]²`, so
  filtering the finite set `piFinset (fun _ => box n)` counts exactly all of them; `c n` is the
  number of n-step self-avoiding walks (c 0 = 1, c 1 = 4, c 2 = 12, ...).
* `c n ≥ 1` for every n (straight walks), so the ratio `c (n+1) / c n` has no junk values.
* `Claim` says the real sequence `c (n+1) / c n` converges to some finite real limit. Since
  `1 ≤ c (n+1)/c n ≤ 3` and by Kesten's theorem/Fekete, any limit is necessarily μ; this is not
  stated. Proving `¬Claim` means the ratio sequence does not converge (e.g. a persistent
  even/odd oscillation).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE113
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical
open Filter Topology

/-- Nearest-neighbour relation on `ℤ²`: ℓ¹-distance exactly 1. -/
def Adj2 (a b : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |a.1 - b.1| + |a.2 - b.2| = 1

/-- The box `[-n,n]²`, which contains every `n`-step walk started at the origin. -/
def box (n : ℕ) : Finset (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  Finset.Icc (-(n : ℤ)) (n : ℤ) ×ˢ Finset.Icc (-(n : ℤ)) (n : ℤ)

/-- The `n`-step self-avoiding walks on `ℤ²` starting at the origin. -/
def saw (n : ℕ) : Finset (Fin (n + 1) → ℤ × ℤ) :=
  (Fintype.piFinset (fun _ : Fin (n + 1) => box n)).filter (fun ω : Fin (n + 1) → ℤ × ℤ =>
    ω 0 = (0, 0) ∧ (∀ i : Fin n, Adj2 (ω i.castSucc) (ω i.succ)) ∧ Function.Injective ω)

/-- Number of `n`-step self-avoiding walks on the square lattice. -/
def c (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (saw n).card

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ L : ℝ, Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (c (n + 1) : ℝ) / (c n : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 L)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE113

title: Planar self-avoiding walk spreads at least diffusively
credit: Madras & Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk (1993); Bauerschmidt, Duminil-Copin, Goodman, Slade, Lectures on Self-Avoiding Walks (2012), Sec. 1.5.2.
premise_risks: Schmidt-Sellke (Feb 2026, unrefereed) technique for self-repelling walks might extend; check before posting
Low novelty: well-known open problem among SAW specialists
plain: Pick one of the self-avoiding n-step walks on the square grid from the origin uniformly at random, and let R_n^2 be the average squared distance of its endpoint from the origin. Intuition says avoiding yourself only pushes you outward, so R_n^2 should be at least of order n, the value for ordinary random walk; physicists expect n^{3/2}. Yet nobody can prove even R_n^2 >= c n for some c > 0: the best proven lower bound is of order n^{2/3}.

Formalization notes:
* An n-step walk on ℤ² from 0 is encoded by its step sequence `s : Fin n → Fin 4`, each step
  being one of the four unit vectors (±1,0), (0,±1) (`dir`). Its vertex after `i` steps is
  `pos s i = ∑_{j < i} dir (s j)`, so `pos s 0 = 0`. This is a bijection with nearest-neighbour
  paths ω : {0,…,n} → ℤ² with ω(0) = 0, and the encoding makes the set of walks a finite type.
* Self-avoiding: `i ↦ pos s i` is injective on `Fin (n+1)` (all n+1 visited vertices distinct).
* `msd n` = (∑ over SAWs of ‖endpoint‖₂²) / #SAWs, as a real number. #SAWs ≥ 1 for every n (the

  so msd n ≥ 1; hence liminf msd n / n > 0 ⇔ ∃ c > 0, ∀ n ≥ 1, msd n ≥ c n (the finitely many

  uniform n-step SAW on ℤ². Proving `¬Claim` = liminf msd n / n = 0 (physically not expected).
  The stronger variant msd n ≥ n is not formalized.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE114
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- The four unit steps of the square lattice. -/
def dir (d : Fin 4) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  if d = 0 then (1, 0) else if d = 1 then (-1, 0) else if d = 2 then (0, 1) else (0, -1)

/-- Position after the first `i` steps of the step sequence `s`. -/
def pos {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → Fin 4) (i : ℕ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => (j : ℕ) < i), dir (s j)

/-- The step sequence `s` is a self-avoiding walk: its `n + 1` vertices are pairwise distinct. -/
def IsSAW {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → Fin 4) : Prop :=
  Function.Injective (fun i : Fin (n + 1) => pos s (i : ℕ))

/-- The finite set of `n`-step self-avoiding walks from the origin. -/
def saw (n : ℕ) : Finset (Fin n → Fin 4) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun s : Fin n → Fin 4 => IsSAW s)

/-- Squared Euclidean norm of a lattice point, as a real. -/
def sqNorm (p : ℤ × ℤ) : ℝ := ((p.1 : ℝ)) ^ 2 + ((p.2 : ℝ)) ^ 2

/-- Mean-square end-to-end displacement of the uniform `n`-step SAW. -/
def msd (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ s ∈ saw n, sqNorm (pos s n)) / ((saw n).card : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → c * (n : ℝ) ≤ msd n

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE114

title: Rotor-router discs: logarithmic outer error
credit: Propp's roundness question; inner/outer bounds and constant-error question from Levine & Peres (2009). The specific O(log r) outer target is my framing as the natural matching step.

plain: Release n chips one at a time at the origin of the square grid. Each grid point has an arrow, all initially pointing east. The n occupied points form a strikingly round disc of radius about r = sqrt(n/pi): simulations up to about 7*10^10 chips show inner and outer radii differing by less than 1.7. Informal statement: Rotor-router aggregation on $\mathbb Z^2$: rotors $\rho:\mathbb Z^2\to\{E,N,W,S\}$
start identically $E$; chips are added one at a time at $0$; a chip at an occupied site advances that
site's rotor one step counterclockwise ($E\to N\to W\to S\to E$) and moves one lattice step in the new
direction, stopping at the first unoccupied site it reaches. Let $A_n$ be the set of occupied sites
after $n$ chips and $r=\sqrt{n/\pi}$. Prove that there is a constant $C$ with
$A_n\subseteq\{z\in\mathbb Z^2:\|z\|_2\le r+C\log(2+r)\}$ for all $n\ge1$.
Formalization notes:
* Sites are `ℤ × ℤ`; a rotor configuration is `ℤ × ℤ → Fin 4` with `0 = E, 1 = N, 2 = W, 3 = S`
  (`dirVec` gives the unit steps (1,0), (0,1), (−1,0), (0,−1)). Counterclockwise advance is `+ 1`
  in `Fin 4` (wraps 3 ↦ 0, i.e. S ↦ E). The initial configuration is constantly `0` (east).
* One walker step `rotorStep` at position p: set ρ(p) := ρ(p) + 1, then move to p + dirVec(ρ(p)+1).
  This is the "rotate, then move" convention of Levine–Peres / Friedrich–Levine.
* One chip (`addChip`): starting from the origin with the current rotors, iterate `rotorStep` and
  stop at the first time k at which the walker's position is unoccupied (time 0 included, so the
  first chip occupies the origin without moving); that site becomes occupied and the rotors are
  those after the k steps. All steps before time k are taken from occupied sites, as required.
  The first exit time is `Nat.find` of the existence statement. It is a standard (and elementary)
  fact that a rotor walk on ℤ² started inside a finite set leaves it in finite time, so the `else`
  branch (state unchanged) is never used; it only makes the definition total and cannot be
  exploited, because it is never reached.
* `A n` = occupied set after n chips (it has exactly n elements). `r n = √(n/π)`.
* Proving `Claim` = an explicit-constant outer bound r + C log(2+r) for this specific (all-east,
  counterclockwise) process, matching the Levine–Peres inner bound. The `log(2 + r)` form avoids the
  degenerate value of log at small n and is equivalent to C log r for large n (small n are absorbed
  into C). Proving `¬Claim` = the outer radius minus r is not O(log r) along some sequence of n.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE115
noncomputable section

/-- Lattice sites. -/
abbrev Cell : Type := ℤ × ℤ

/-- Rotor configurations: `0 = E, 1 = N, 2 = W, 3 = S`. -/
abbrev Rotors : Type := Cell → Fin 4

/-- Unit step in direction `d` (E, N, W, S). -/
def dirVec (d : Fin 4) : Cell := ![((1 : ℤ), (0 : ℤ)), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1)] d

/-- One walker step: advance the rotor at the current site counterclockwise, then move along it. -/
def rotorStep (c : Rotors × Cell) : Rotors × Cell :=
  (Function.update c.1 c.2 (c.1 c.2 + 1), c.2 + dirVec (c.1 c.2 + 1))

/-- The walker (rotors, position) after `k` steps, started at the origin with rotors `ρ`. -/
def chipWalk (ρ : Rotors) (k : ℕ) : Rotors × Cell :=
  rotorStep^[k] (ρ, ((0 : ℤ), (0 : ℤ)))

open scoped Classical in
/-- Add one chip: it walks until the first time it is at an unoccupied site, which it occupies. -/
def addChip (s : Rotors × Set Cell) : Rotors × Set Cell :=
  if h : ∃ k : ℕ, (chipWalk s.1 k).2 ∉ s.2 then
    ((chipWalk s.1 (Nat.find h)).1, insert (chipWalk s.1 (Nat.find h)).2 s.2)
  else s

/-- State after `n` chips, starting from all rotors east and nothing occupied. -/
def config (n : ℕ) : Rotors × Set Cell :=
  addChip^[n] ((fun _ : Cell => (0 : Fin 4)), (∅ : Set Cell))

/-- The rotor-router aggregate `A_n`. -/
def A (n : ℕ) : Set Cell := (config n).2

/-- `r = √(n/π)`. -/
def r (n : ℕ) : ℝ := Real.sqrt ((n : ℝ) / Real.pi)

/-- Euclidean norm of a lattice site. -/
def euclNorm (z : Cell) : ℝ := Real.sqrt (((z.1 : ℝ)) ^ 2 + ((z.2 : ℝ)) ^ 2)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∀ z ∈ A n, euclNorm z ≤ r n + C * Real.log (2 + r n)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE115

title: Square-lattice polygon counts satisfy no polynomial recurrence
credit: Guttmann-Enting solvability criterion; open question recorded by Rechnitzer (2006).
premise_risks: May be very hard (essentially requires structural control of an unsolved model)
Formalizing 'polygon modulo translation' needs care (cyclic, unoriented, rooted at lexicographically least vertex)
plain: Let p_n count closed self-avoiding loops of length 2n on the square grid, up to translation (p_2 = 1, p_3 = 2, p_4 = 7, p_5 = 28, ...). Many solved lattice models have counting sequences that obey a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients (their generating function is 'D-finite'). For square-lattice polygons it is believed that no such recurrence exists, reflecting that the model has no exact solution of this kind. Prove it.
math: Let $p_n$ be the number of self-avoiding polygons (unrooted, unoriented closed nearest-neighbour cycles) of perimeter $2n$ on $\mathbb Z^2$, counted modulo translation, so $p_1=0$, $p_2=1,p_3=2,p_4=7$. Prove that there are no $k\ge0$ and polynomials $Q_0,\dots,Q_k\in\mathbb Q[x]$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i=0}^k Q_i(n)\,p_{n+i}=0$ for all $n\ge1$. Equivalently, $P(x)=\sum_n p_nx^n$ is not D-finite.

/-! QED-E116: Square-lattice polygon counts satisfy no polynomial recurrence
Let p_n count closed self-avoiding loops of length 2n on the square grid, up to translation (p_2 = 1, p_3 = 2, p_4 = 7, p_5 = 28, ...). Many solved lattice models have counting sequences that obey a linear recurrence with polynomial coefficients (their generating function is 'D-finite'). For square-lattice polygons it is believed that no such recurrence exists, reflecting that the model has no exact solution of this kind. Prove it.
Informal statement: Let $p_n$ be the number of self-avoiding polygons (unrooted, unoriented closed nearest-neighbour cycles) of perimeter $2n$ on $\mathbb Z^2$, counted modulo translation, so $p_1=0$, $p_2=1,p_3=2,p_4=7$. Prove that there are no $k\ge0$ and polynomials $Q_0,\dots,Q_k\in\mathbb Q[x]$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i=0}^k Q_i(n)\,p_{n+i}=0$ for all $n\ge1$. Equivalently, $P(x)=\sum_n p_nx^n$ is not D-finite.
Formalization notes:
* `Adj2` is the square-lattice nearest-neighbour relation (ℓ¹-distance 1).
* `rooted m` is the finite set of injective maps `ω : Fin m → ℤ × ℤ` with `ω 0 = (0,0)` (written
  `∀ h : 0 < m, ω ⟨0, h⟩ = (0,0)` to avoid needing `NeZero m`) and cyclic adjacency
  `Adj2 (ω i) (ω (finRotate m i))`, where `finRotate m i = i+1 mod m`. All such vertices lie in
  the box `[-m,m]²`, so the `piFinset` filter counts all of them.
* For `m = 2n ≥ 4`, such an `ω` is exactly a self-avoiding polygon with `2n` edges together with a
  choice of starting vertex (translated to the origin) and a direction of traversal; each polygon
  modulo translation gives exactly `2n · 2` distinct such `ω` (reversal gives a different sequence
  since the cycle has at least 4 vertices). Hence `p n = #rooted (2n) / (4n)` for `n ≥ 2`
  (computed in ℚ; the division is exact). For `n ≤ 1` there is no polygon (an injective length-2
  "cycle" is a back-and-forth step, not a polygon), so `p 0 = p 1 = 0` is set by hand.
  Check: `#rooted 4 = 8`, so `p 2 = 1`.
* `Claim` is the negation of P-recursiveness: no `k` and no family `Q : Fin (k+1) → ℚ[x]`, not all
  zero, with `∑ᵢ Qᵢ(n) p(n+i) = 0` for all `n ≥ 1`. This is the standard definition; requiring
  the recurrence for all `n ≥ 1` rather than for all large `n` is equivalent (multiply the
  `Qᵢ` by a polynomial vanishing at the finitely many exceptional `n`), as is the choice of
  values `p 0`, `p 1`. P-recursiveness of `(p n)` is equivalent to D-finiteness of `∑ p_n xⁿ`.
  Proving `Claim` = the isotropic SAP generating function is not D-finite; `¬Claim` = it is.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE116
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Nearest-neighbour relation on `ℤ²`: ℓ¹-distance exactly 1. -/
def Adj2 (a b : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |a.1 - b.1| + |a.2 - b.2| = 1

/-- The box `[-m,m]²`. -/
def box (m : ℕ) : Finset (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  Finset.Icc (-(m : ℤ)) (m : ℤ) ×ˢ Finset.Icc (-(m : ℤ)) (m : ℤ)

/-- Rooted, oriented self-avoiding cycles of length `m` through the origin, as injective cyclic
nearest-neighbour sequences starting at the origin. -/
def rooted (m : ℕ) : Finset (Fin m → ℤ × ℤ) :=
  (Fintype.piFinset (fun _ : Fin m => box m)).filter (fun ω : Fin m → ℤ × ℤ =>
    (∀ h : 0 < m, ω ⟨0, h⟩ = (0, 0)) ∧
    (∀ i : Fin m, Adj2 (ω i) (ω (finRotate m i))) ∧ Function.Injective ω)

/-- Number of self-avoiding polygons of perimeter `2n` on `ℤ²` modulo translation. -/
def p (n : ℕ) : ℚ :=
  if 2 ≤ n then ((rooted (2 * n)).card : ℚ) / (4 * (n : ℚ)) else 0

def Claim : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ (k : ℕ) (Q : Fin (k + 1) → Polynomial ℚ), (∃ i : Fin (k + 1), Q i ≠ 0) ∧
    ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n → ∑ i : Fin (k + 1), (Q i).eval (n : ℚ) * p (n + (i : ℕ)) = 0

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE116

title: Does a Moore graph of degree 57 exist?
credit: Hoffman and Singleton (1960); recent restrictions by Mačaj–Širáň, Smith–Montemanni, and others
premise_risks: Very famous problem: low novelty, high difficulty
'Moore graph' is a person-named object, but the question is not a named conjecture
Two 2026 partial-result papers are recent (one arXiv only); they do not affect the open status
plain: A Moore graph of diameter 2 is a regular graph in which any two vertices are either adjacent or have exactly one common neighbour; with degree k it has k^2+1 vertices, the most a diameter-2 graph of degree k can have. Hoffman and Singleton (1960) showed such graphs can exist only for k = 2, 3, 7, 57, and the first three exist (pentagon, Petersen graph, Hoffman-Singleton graph). Does one exist for degree 57, with 3250 vertices?
math: Decide whether there exists a simple graph $G$ on $3250$ vertices that is $57$-regular, triangle-free, and in which every two distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbour; equivalently, whether a strongly regular graph with parameters $(3250,57,0,1)$ exists.

A Moore graph of diameter 2 is a regular graph in which any two vertices are either adjacent or have exactly one common neighbour; with degree k it has k^2+1 vertices, the most a diameter-2 graph of degree k can have. Hoffman and Singleton (1960) showed such graphs can exist only for k = 2, 3, 7, 57, and the first three exist (pentagon, Petersen graph, Hoffman-Singleton graph). Does one exist for degree 57, with 3250 vertices?
Informal statement: Decide whether there exists a simple graph $G$ on $3250$ vertices that is $57$-regular, triangle-free, and in which every two distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbour; equivalently, whether a strongly regular graph with parameters $(3250,57,0,1)$ exists.
Formalization notes:
* Graphs on 3250 vertices are `SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)` (every 3250-vertex graph is isomorphic
  to one of these). Degrees and common-neighbour counts are cardinalities of explicit filters of
  `Finset.univ` (classical decidability), so no `DecidableRel` instance needs to be supplied.
* `IsMoore57 G`: every vertex has exactly 57 neighbours; no triangle (adjacent vertices have no
  common neighbour, i.e. λ = 0); distinct non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common
  neighbour (μ = 1). This is precisely an srg(3250, 57, 0, 1), i.e. a Moore graph of degree 57
  and diameter 2 (diameter ≤ 2 follows from μ = 1; the graph is not complete).
* This is a decision problem. Proving `Claim` = exhibiting (constructing) such a graph.
  Proving `¬Claim` = showing no Moore graph of degree 57 exists.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE117
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- Neighbourhood of `v` in `G`, as a finset. -/
def nbhd (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)) (v : Fin 3250) : Finset (Fin 3250) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun w : Fin 3250 => G.Adj v w)

/-- Common neighbours of `u` and `v`. -/
def common (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)) (u v : Fin 3250) : Finset (Fin 3250) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun w : Fin 3250 => G.Adj u w ∧ G.Adj v w)

/-- `G` is a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1), i.e. a Moore graph of
degree 57 and diameter 2. -/
def IsMoore57 (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250)) : Prop :=
  (∀ v : Fin 3250, (nbhd G v).card = 57) ∧
  (∀ u v : Fin 3250, G.Adj u v → (common G u v).card = 0) ∧
  (∀ u v : Fin 3250, u ≠ v → ¬ G.Adj u v → (common G u v).card = 1)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3250), IsMoore57 G

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE117

title: Sylver coinage: who wins after the opening 16?
credit: Conway (game and prize problem); Berlekamp–Conway–Guy, Winning Ways; Guy (1976); Sicherman (2002)
premise_risks: Appears in Conway's prize list; it is not usually called a named conjecture, but some readers may call it 'Conway's 16 problem'

Which player wins if the first player opens with 16?
math: A position is a finite set $S\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}$; a legal move from $S$ is any integer $n\ge 2$ not in the additive monoid $\langle S\rangle$, giving $S\cup\{n\}$. Under normal play the player with no legal move loses (this matches the rule that naming $1$ loses). Every play is finite, by Dickson's lemma. lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-E118: Sylver coinage: who wins after the opening 16?
In Sylver coinage two players take turns naming positive integers. You may not name a number that can be written as a sum of numbers already named (repeats allowed), and whoever names 1 loses. Every prime 5 or larger is a winning first move. Any other winning first move must have the form 2^a 3^b, and the openings 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 are known to lose. Which player wins if the first player opens with 16?
Informal statement: A position is a finite set $S\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}$; a legal move from $S$ is any integer
$n\ge 2$ not in the additive monoid $\langle S\rangle$, giving $S\cup\{n\}$. Under normal play the player with no
legal move loses (this matches the rule that naming $1$ loses). Every play is finite, by Dickson's lemma.
Decide whether $\{16\}$ is a $\mathcal P$-position (the player who named $16$ wins) or an $\mathcal N$-position.
Formalization notes:
* Positions are `Finset ℕ` (the numbers named so far); `⟨S⟩` is `AddSubmonoid.closure (S : Set ℕ)`,
  the set of sums of elements of `S` with repetition (it contains 0, which is harmless since moves
  are `≥ 2`).
* Moves: `Legal S n ↔ 2 ≤ n ∧ n ∉ ⟨S⟩`. Naming 1 (legal in the original game while `1 ∉ ⟨S⟩`)
  loses immediately, so no player names 1 while another move exists, and a player with no move
  `≥ 2` is forced to name 1 and loses: this is exactly normal play on moves `≥ 2`.
* `PLose S` (the player to move from `S` loses under optimal play) is the inductive (least
  fixed point) predicate: every legal `n` has a legal reply `m` with `PLose (S ∪ {n, m})`.
  Terminal positions satisfy it vacuously. Being inductive, `PLose S` asserts that the
  second player can force a win in finitely many moves; since every play is finite (each move
  strictly enlarges `⟨S⟩`, and ℕ has the ascending chain condition on submonoids), this is the
  game-theoretic outcome, and every position is exactly one of `PLose` or
  `NWin S := ∃ n, Legal S n ∧ PLose (insert n S)` (determinacy, provable by well-founded induction).
* The opening 16 is the position `{16}` with the second player to move. `Claim := PLose {16}`,
  i.e. `{16}` is a 𝒫-position: the first player, having named 16, wins. Proving `¬Claim`
  (equivalently, by determinacy, `NWin {16}`) = the second player has a winning reply, i.e. 16 is a
  losing opening. Either proof settles the problem; the choice of polarity is not a conjecture.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE118
noncomputable section

/-- A legal move from position `S`: an integer `n ≥ 2` that is not a sum of named numbers. -/
def Legal (S : Finset ℕ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  2 ≤ n ∧ n ∉ AddSubmonoid.closure (S : Set ℕ)

/-- One step of the losing-position rule: every legal move `n` from `S` has a legal reply `m`
after which the position is again in `P`. -/
def LoseStep (P : Finset ℕ → Prop) (S : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, Legal S n → ∃ m : ℕ, Legal (insert n S) m ∧ P (insert m (insert n S))

/-- `PLose S`: the player to move from `S` loses (normal play, moves `≥ 2`). Defined as the
least fixed point of `LoseStep` (impredicative encoding of the inductive definition
`LoseStep PLose S → PLose S`, which Lean rejects as a nested inductive through `∃`). -/
def PLose (S : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ P : Finset ℕ → Prop, (∀ T, LoseStep P T → P T) → P S

/-- `NWin S`: the player to move from `S` has a winning move. -/
def NWin (S : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ n : ℕ, Legal S n ∧ PLose (insert n S)

/-- After the opening `16`, the second player (to move) loses: `16` is a winning opening. -/
def Claim : Prop := PLose {16}

Decide whether Breaker has a strategy such that, against every Maker strategy, Maker never owns all cells of any winning line. (The analogous question for $k=6$ is also open.)

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E119: Maker-Breaker 7-in-a-row on the infinite grid
Two players take turns claiming cells of the infinite square grid. Maker wins if she ever owns k
consecutive cells in a row, column or diagonal, and Breaker wins if he stops this forever. Maker
wins for k <= 5, and Breaker wins for k >= 8 with a pairing strategy. Does Breaker win for k = 7?
Informal statement: Maker and Breaker alternately claim one unclaimed cell of $\mathbb Z^2$, Maker
first. A winning line is a set $\{p+i d:0\le i<7\}$ with $p\in\mathbb Z^2$ and
$d\in\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,-1)\}$. Decide whether Breaker has a strategy such that, against every
Maker strategy, Maker never owns all cells of any winning line.
Formalization notes:
* Cells are `ℤ × ℤ`. A play is an infinite sequence of moves; move number t (t = 0, 1, 2, …) is
  Maker's if t is even and Breaker's if t is odd (Maker first).
* A (pure, full-information) strategy is a function from the history so far to a cell. The history
  is the list of effective moves `Option (ℤ × ℤ)` in chronological order (`none` = pass). Both
  players see the whole history, as in any perfect-information game.
* Illegal moves (choosing an already-claimed cell) are converted into passes. This does not change
  who wins: a pass is never better than a legal move in a Maker-Breaker game (an extra claimed cell
  never hurts its owner), and a legal move always exists since only finitely many cells are claimed
  at any time. So a Breaker strategy that wins with passes allowed can be converted into a legal
  one, and Maker strategies with passes are dominated by legal ones.
* Maker owns a cell iff she claimed it at some (even) time; "Maker ever owns a whole winning line"
  is therefore "every cell of the line is in Maker's set over the whole infinite play". Since cells
  are never lost, this is the same as owning the line at some finite time.
* `Claim` = Breaker has a winning strategy for k = 7: ∃ σB, ∀ σM, no winning line is all Maker's.
  `¬Claim` = for every Breaker strategy some Maker strategy completes a line; by Gale–Stewart
  determinacy (Maker's winning set is open) this is equivalent to Maker having a winning strategy.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE119
noncomputable section

/-- Cells of the board. -/
abbrev Cell : Type := ℤ × ℤ

/-- A strategy: next cell as a function of the history of effective moves (`none` = pass). -/
abbrev Strategy : Type := List (Option Cell) → Cell

open scoped Classical in
/-- The effective next move after history `h`: the player to move is Maker iff `h` has even
length; an already-claimed cell becomes a pass. -/
def effMove (σM σB : Strategy) (h : List (Option Cell)) : Option Cell :=
  let c : Cell := if h.length % 2 = 0 then σM h else σB h
  if some c ∈ h then none else some c

/-- History after `t` moves. -/
def hist (σM σB : Strategy) : ℕ → List (Option Cell)
  | 0 => []
  | t + 1 => hist σM σB t ++ [effMove σM σB (hist σM σB t)]

/-- Maker claims `c` at some point of the play. -/
def MakerOwns (σM σB : Strategy) (c : Cell) : Prop :=
  ∃ t : ℕ, t % 2 = 0 ∧ effMove σM σB (hist σM σB t) = some c

/-- The four line directions. -/
def dirs : Set Cell := {((1 : ℤ), (0 : ℤ)), (0, 1), (1, 1), (1, -1)}

/-- The winning line of length 7 starting at `p` in direction `d`, cell `i`. -/
def lineCell (p d : Cell) (i : ℕ) : Cell :=
  (p.1 + (i : ℤ) * d.1, p.2 + (i : ℤ) * d.2)

/-- Breaker wins the play: Maker never owns a whole winning line. -/
def BreakerWinsPlay (σM σB : Strategy) : Prop :=
  ∀ p : Cell, ∀ d ∈ dirs, ¬ ∀ i : ℕ, i < 7 → MakerOwns σM σB (lineCell p d i)

def Claim : Prop := ∃ σB : Strategy, ∀ σM : Strategy, BreakerWinsPlay σM σB

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE119

Decide whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=O(n^{5/3})$, i.e. whether $\limsup_n \mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})/n^{5/3}<\infty$. (Stronger target: $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=\Theta(n^{7/4})$.)

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E120: Does ex(n, K_{4,4}) grow faster than n^{5/3}?
How many edges can a graph on n vertices have if it contains no complete bipartite graph K_{4,4}? The general upper bound is of order n^{7/4}. The best known constructions give only order n^{5/3}, which is already achieved by graphs that avoid the smaller K_{3,3}. Can one do better than a constant times n^{5/3}?
Informal statement: Let $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})$ be the maximum number of edges in a $K_{4,4}$-free graph on $n$ vertices. Known: $c\,n^{5/3}\le\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})\le C\,n^{7/4}$. Decide whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=O(n^{5/3})$, i.e. whether $\limsup_n \mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})/n^{5/3}<\infty$. (Stronger target: $\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{4,4})=\Theta(n^{7/4})$.)
Formalization notes:
* A simple graph `G` on `Fin n` contains `K_{4,4}` (as a not necessarily induced subgraph) iff
  there are disjoint 4-sets `A`, `B` with every `a ∈ A` adjacent to every `b ∈ B`; `K44Free G`
  is the negation.
* `edgeCount G` counts pairs `(i,j)` with `i < j` and `G.Adj i j`, i.e. the number of edges
  (each edge counted once). `ex n` is the maximum of `edgeCount` over the finite set of
  `K_{4,4}`-free graphs on `Fin n` (a `Finset.sup` over a nonempty set, since the empty graph
  is `K_{4,4}`-free, so it is a genuine maximum).
* `Claim`: `ex(n, K_{4,4})` is not `O(n^{5/3})`, i.e. there is no `C` with
  `ex n ≤ C n^{5/3}` for all `n` (real power `n ^ (5/3 : ℝ)`; at `n = 0` both sides are `0`).
  This is exactly "one can do better than a constant times `n^{5/3}`" (equivalently
  `limsup ex n / n^{5/3} = ∞`). Proving `¬Claim` means `ex(n, K_{4,4}) = O(n^{5/3})`, which with
  the known lower bound gives `ex(n, K_{4,4}) = Θ(n^{5/3})`. Both sides are genuine answers.
  The stronger target `Θ(n^{7/4})` is not formalized.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE120
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical
open Filter

/-- `G` contains no copy of `K_{4,4}`. -/
def K44Free {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ A B : Finset (Fin n), A.card = 4 ∧ B.card = 4 ∧ Disjoint A B ∧
    ∀ a ∈ A, ∀ b ∈ B, G.Adj a b

/-- Number of edges of `G`. -/
def edgeCount {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n × Fin n)).filter
    (fun q : Fin n × Fin n => q.1 < q.2 ∧ G.Adj q.1 q.2)).card

/-- The Turán number `ex(n, K_{4,4})`. -/
def ex (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (SimpleGraph (Fin n))).filter
    (fun G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) => K44Free G)).sup (fun G : SimpleGraph (Fin n) => edgeCount G)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, (ex n : ℝ) ≤ C * (n : ℝ) ^ ((5 : ℝ) / 3)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE120

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E121: Linear arboricity of graphs with maximum degree 7
A linear forest is a graph whose components are paths. The linear arboricity conjecture says the edges of any graph with maximum degree D can be split into ceil((D+1)/2) linear forests. It was proved for D = 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 by 1988, but D = 7 is the smallest open case. Can the edges of every graph with maximum degree 7 be split into 4 linear forests?
Informal statement: Prove or disprove: every finite simple graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\le 7$ admits a map $c:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}$ such that every colour class is a linear forest (acyclic, with maximum degree at most $2$). Equivalently, $\mathrm{la}(G)\le 4$ whenever $\Delta(G)\le 7$.
Formalization notes:
* Finite simple graphs are `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` for `n : ℕ` (every finite graph is isomorphic
  to one of these). Degrees are cards of classical filters of `Finset.univ`.
* A linear forest is a graph that is acyclic (`SimpleGraph.IsAcyclic`: no walk that is a cycle)
  with every vertex of degree ≤ 2; equivalently every component is a path (isolated vertices
  are trivial paths). This is the standard definition.
* A colouring is any function `c : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 4`; only its values on `G.edgeSet` matter.
  Colour class `i` is the graph `fromEdgeSet {e ∈ G.edgeSet | c e = i}` (a spanning subgraph of
  `G`), so the four classes partition the edges of `G`.
* Proving `Claim` = the linear arboricity conjecture for Δ = 7 (then 4 is tight, since 7-regular
  graphs need 4 linear forests). Proving `¬Claim` = a finite graph with Δ ≤ 7 whose edges cannot
  be split into 4 linear forests (a counterexample to the linear arboricity conjecture).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE121
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- Degree of `v` in a graph on `Fin n`. -/
def deg {n : ℕ} (H : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (v : Fin n) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun w : Fin n => H.Adj v w)).card

/-- A linear forest: acyclic with maximum degree at most 2 (components are paths). -/
def IsLinearForest {n : ℕ} (H : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  H.IsAcyclic ∧ ∀ v : Fin n, deg H v ≤ 2

/-- Colour class `i` of the edge colouring `c` of `G`. -/
def colourClass {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (c : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 4) (i : Fin 4) :
    SimpleGraph (Fin n) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {e : Sym2 (Fin n) | e ∈ G.edgeSet ∧ c e = i}

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), (∀ v : Fin n, deg G v ≤ 7) →
    ∃ c : Sym2 (Fin n) → Fin 4, ∀ i : Fin 4, IsLinearForest (colourClass G c i)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE121
