import Mathlib
/-! QED-E122: The domination game 3/5 bound for all isolate-free graphs
In the domination game on a graph, Dominator and Staller take turns choosing vertices. Each chosen vertex must dominate (be, or be adjacent to) at least one vertex not yet dominated, and the game ends when every vertex is dominated. Dominator wants the game to be short and Staller wants it long. With Dominator moving first and optimal play, does the game always end within 3n/5 moves on an n-vertex graph with no isolated vertices?
Informal statement: For a finite graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with no isolated vertex, let $\gamma_g(G)$ be the
number of moves under optimal play: players alternately choose a vertex $v$ with $N[v]\not\subseteq N[S]$, where
$S$ is the set of vertices chosen so far; Dominator moves first and minimizes the length, Staller maximizes it, and
the game ends when $N[S]=V(G)$. Prove or disprove $\gamma_g(G)\le 3n/5$. Best known: $\gamma_g(G)\le 5n/8$.
Formalization notes:
* Graphs: `G : SimpleGraph V` with `V : Type` finite (`Fintype V`), `n = Fintype.card V`.
  No isolated vertex: `∀ v, ∃ u, G.Adj v u`.
* State: the set `D = N[S] ⊆ V` of dominated vertices (all that matters for legality and
  termination) and whose turn it is (`true` = Dominator). Closed neighbourhood
  `cnbhd G v = {v} ∪ N(v)`. A move `v` is legal iff `¬ cnbhd G v ⊆ D`; it updates
  `D ↦ D ∪ cnbhd G v`. The game ends when `D = univ`.
* `CanFinish G b D k` ("Dominator can force the game from state `(D, b)` to end within `k`
  further moves"), by recursion on `k`: with `k = 0` the game must already be over; with
  `k+1`, either it is over, or (Dominator to move) some legal move leads to `CanFinish … k`, or
  (Staller to move) every legal move does. Staller is never vacuously stuck: if `D ≠ univ`,
  any undominated `u` is a legal move. Thus `γ_g(G) ≤ k ↔ CanFinish G true ∅ k` (standard
  min–max over the finite game tree, which has depth ≤ n).
* Since `γ_g(G)` is an integer, `γ_g(G) ≤ 3n/5 ↔ γ_g(G) ≤ ⌊3n/5⌋ = 3 * n / 5` (ℕ division).
* `Claim` = the 3/5 conjecture (Kinnersley–West–Zamani) for all isolate-free graphs.
  `¬Claim` = a finite isolate-free graph with `γ_g(G) > 3n/5`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE122
noncomputable section

variable {V : Type}

/-- Closed neighbourhood `N[v] = {v} ∪ N(v)`. -/
def cnbhd (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Set V := {u : V | u = v ∨ G.Adj v u}

/-- `CanFinish G b D k`: from dominated set `D` with Dominator to move iff `b = true`,
Dominator can force the domination game to end within `k` more moves. -/
def CanFinish (G : SimpleGraph V) : Bool → Set V → ℕ → Prop
  | _, D, 0 => D = Set.univ
  | true, D, k + 1 =>
      D = Set.univ ∨ ∃ v : V, ¬ cnbhd G v ⊆ D ∧ CanFinish G false (D ∪ cnbhd G v) k
  | false, D, k + 1 =>
      D = Set.univ ∨ ∀ v : V, ¬ cnbhd G v ⊆ D → CanFinish G true (D ∪ cnbhd G v) k

/-- The 3/5 conjecture: `γ_g(G) ≤ 3n/5` for every finite graph without isolated vertices. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V), (∀ v : V, ∃ u : V, G.Adj v u) →
    CanFinish G true (∅ : Set V) (3 * Fintype.card V / 5)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE122

title: Threshold bias of the Maker-Breaker triangle game
credit: Chvátal and Erdős (1978); Balogh–Samotij; Glazik–Srivastav

plain: On the edges of the complete graph K_n, Maker claims one edge per turn and Breaker claims q edges per turn; Maker wins if she ever owns a triangle. Let q_0(n) be the smallest q for which Breaker wins. It is known that q_0(n) lies between about 1.414 sqrt(n) and 1.633 sqrt(n). What is the right constant, conjecturally sqrt(2)? As a concrete step, can either bound be improved by a constant factor?

Prove that one of the two bounds can be improved by a constant factor: either there is $c'<\sqrt{8/3}$ with $q_0(n)\le c'\sqrt n$ for all large $n$, or there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $q_0(n)\ge(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)\sqrt n$ for all large $n$.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E123: Threshold bias of the Maker-Breaker triangle game
On the edges of the complete graph K_n, Maker claims one edge per turn and Breaker claims q edges per
turn; Maker wins if she ever owns a triangle. Let q_0(n) be the smallest q for which Breaker wins. It
is known that q_0(n) lies between about 1.414 sqrt(n) and 1.633 sqrt(n). What is the right constant,
conjecturally sqrt(2)? As a concrete step, can either bound be improved by a constant factor?
Informal statement: Let $q_0(n)$ be the least $q$ such that Breaker wins the $(1:q)$ Maker-Breaker
triangle game on $E(K_n)$ (Maker first). Known:
$(\sqrt2-o(1))\sqrt n\le q_0(n)\le(\sqrt{8/3}+o(1))\sqrt n$. Prove that one of the two bounds can be
improved by a constant factor: either there is $c'<\sqrt{8/3}$ with $q_0(n)\le c'\sqrt n$ for all
large $n$, or there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $q_0(n)\ge(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)\sqrt n$ for all large $n$.
(The full problem, determining $\lim q_0(n)/\sqrt n$, is not a single proposition; this is the
"concrete target" of the source, stated as one disjunction.)
Formalization notes:
* Edges of K_n: the non-diagonal elements of `Sym2 (Fin n)` (`allEdges n`). A position is the pair
  (M, B) of Maker's and Breaker's edge sets. One round: Maker picks an edge, then Breaker picks a
  set of edges.
* Strategies are positional: Maker's is `(M, B) ↦ edge`, Breaker's is `(M, B) ↦ set of edges`
  (Breaker sees Maker's new edge). This is without loss of generality: the continuation of the game
  depends only on the position, so by backward induction the winner of this finite game has a
  positional winning strategy, and against a fixed positional Breaker strategy any
  history-dependent Maker play can be replayed by a positional Maker strategy (positions strictly
  grow except in rounds where nothing happens, which can be cut out).
* Illegal moves become passes: Maker's edge counts only if it is unclaimed; Breaker's set is
  intersected with the unclaimed edges and counts only if it has at most q elements. Claiming fewer
  edges never helps a player in a Maker-Breaker game, so allowing "at most q" and passes gives the
  same winner as the standard rule "exactly q, or all remaining edges if fewer". In particular
  `BreakerWins n q` is monotone in q. Rounds are iterated forever; once all edges are claimed the
  position is constant.
* Maker wins iff at some time her edges contain a triangle. `BreakerWins n q` = some Breaker
  strategy prevents this against all Maker strategies.
* `q0 n = sInf {q | BreakerWins n q}`; the set is nonempty (q = number of edges of K_n: Breaker
  takes everything after Maker's first edge), so there is no junk value.
* Proving `Claim` = an explicit constant-factor improvement of the Glazik–Srivastav upper bound
  or of the Chvátal–Erdős lower bound. `¬Claim` = both bounds are asymptotically sharp along
  subsequences: for every c' < √(8/3), q0 n > c'√n infinitely often, and for every ε > 0,
  q0 n < (√2+ε)√n infinitely often.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE123
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Edges of `K_n`. -/
def allEdges (n : ℕ) : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) := Finset.univ.filter fun e => ¬ e.IsDiag

/-- Positional Maker strategy. -/
abbrev MakerStrategy (n : ℕ) : Type := Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) → Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) → Sym2 (Fin n)

/-- Positional Breaker strategy. -/
abbrev BreakerStrategy (n : ℕ) : Type :=
  Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) → Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) → Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))

/-- One round of the `(1 : q)` game from position `(M, B)`. -/
def playRound (n q : ℕ) (σM : MakerStrategy n) (σB : BreakerStrategy n)
    (P : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) × Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))) :
    Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) × Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) :=
  let M := P.1
  let B := P.2
  let e := σM M B
  let M' := if e ∈ allEdges n \ (M ∪ B) then insert e M else M
  let S := σB M' B ∩ (allEdges n \ (M' ∪ B))
  let B' := if S.card ≤ q then B ∪ S else B
  (M', B')

/-- Position after `t` rounds. -/
def gamePos (n q : ℕ) (σM : MakerStrategy n) (σB : BreakerStrategy n) (t : ℕ) :
    Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) × Finset (Sym2 (Fin n)) :=
  (playRound n q σM σB)^[t] (∅, ∅)

/-- The edge set contains a triangle. -/
def HasTriangle {n : ℕ} (M : Finset (Sym2 (Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b c : Fin n, a ≠ b ∧ b ≠ c ∧ a ≠ c ∧ s(a, b) ∈ M ∧ s(b, c) ∈ M ∧ s(a, c) ∈ M

/-- Breaker wins the `(1 : q)` triangle game on `K_n`. -/
def BreakerWins (n q : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ σB : BreakerStrategy n, ∀ σM : MakerStrategy n, ∀ t : ℕ,
    ¬ HasTriangle (gamePos n q σM σB t).1

/-- The threshold bias `q_0(n)`. -/
def q0 (n : ℕ) : ℕ := sInf {q : ℕ | BreakerWins n q}

def Claim : Prop :=
  (∃ c' : ℝ, c' < Real.sqrt (8 / 3) ∧
      ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, (q0 n : ℝ) ≤ c' * Real.sqrt n) ∨
  (∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧
      ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, (Real.sqrt 2 + ε) * Real.sqrt n ≤ (q0 n : ℝ))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE123

/-! QED-E124: Separating words below the cube-root barrier
Given two different binary words of the same length n, how small a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is needed to accept one and reject the other? The best known upper bound is about n^{1/3} states and the best lower bound is only about log n. Prove that O(n^c) states always suffice for some exponent c < 1/3.
Informal statement: For distinct $u,v\in\{0,1\}^n$ let $\mathrm{sep}(u,v)$ be the least number of states of a DFA over $\{0,1\}$ that accepts exactly one of $u,v$, and let $S(n)=\max\{\mathrm{sep}(u,v):u\ne v,\ |u|=|v|=n\}$. Prove that there exist $c<1/3$ and $C>0$ with $S(n)\le C\,n^{c}$ for all $n\ge2$. (Known: $\Omega(\log n)\le S(n)\le O(n^{1/3}\log^{7}n)$; the conjectured truth is $S(n)=O(\log n)$.)
Formalization notes:
* DFAs are Mathlib's `DFA Bool (Fin k)` (complete deterministic automata: total transition
  function `step`, start state, accepting set), evaluated by `DFA.eval` (left fold of `step`
  from `start`). Binary words are `List Bool`. A DFA with state type `Fin k` has exactly `k`
  states (k ≥ 1 automatically, as `start : Fin k`).
* "Some DFA with exactly k states separates u, v" is monotone in k (add unreachable states),
  so `S(n) ≤ C n^c` ⇔ for all distinct u, v of length n there is k ≤ C n^c and a k-state DFA
  accepting exactly one of u, v. This is the form used in `Claim`.
* `n ^ c` is `Real.rpow` with base n ≥ 2 > 0; c is any real < 1/3 (negative c would only make
  the claim stronger and is in fact impossible since S(n) ≥ 2).
* Proving `Claim` = a polynomial improvement of the exponent 1/3 (Chase). Proving `¬Claim` =
  S(n) is not O(n^c) for any c < 1/3 (would refute the O(log n) conjecture).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE124
noncomputable section

/-- Some DFA with `k` states over `{0,1}` accepts exactly one of `u` and `v`. -/
def Separates (k : ℕ) (u v : List Bool) : Prop :=
  ∃ M : DFA Bool (Fin k), ¬ (M.eval u ∈ M.accept ↔ M.eval v ∈ M.accept)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, c < 1 / 3 ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧
    ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n → ∀ u v : List Bool, u.length = n → v.length = n → u ≠ v →
      ∃ k : ℕ, (k : ℝ) ≤ C * (n : ℝ) ^ c ∧ Separates k u v

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE124

title: A subcubic bound for reset words
credit: Unnamed weakening of the Černý conjecture; bounds by Pin, Frankl, Szykuła, Shitov.
premise_risks: Must ensure no 2026 preprint claims a subcubic or quadratic general bound (none found).
Some may view it as a famous problem in disguise, but it is a strictly weaker, separately-stated open question.
plain: A finite automaton is synchronizing if some input word sends every state to one and the same state; the shortest such word is called a reset word. For automata with n states the shortest reset word is conjectured to have length at most (n-1)^2, but the best proven bound is still about n^3/6. Prove any bound that is asymptotically smaller than n^3.
math: For a complete DFA $\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, call $w\in\Sigma^*$ reset if $|\delta(Q,w)|=1$; let $\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)$ be the length of a shortest reset word, and $C(n)=\max\{\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A): |Q|=n,\ \mathcal A\text{ synchronizing},\ \Sigma\text{ finite}\}$ (finite, since $\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)<2^n$). Prove $C(n)=o(n^3)$. (Known: $(n-1)^2\le C(n)\le(7/48+15625/798768)\,n^3+o(n^3)\approx0.1654\,n^3$.)

/-! QED-E125: A subcubic bound for reset words
A finite automaton is synchronizing if some input word sends every state to one and the same state; the shortest such word is called a reset word. For automata with n states the shortest reset word is conjectured to have length at most (n-1)^2, but the best proven bound is still about n^3/6. Prove any bound that is asymptotically smaller than n^3.
Informal statement: For a complete DFA $\mathcal A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, call
$w\in\Sigma^*$ reset if $|\delta(Q,w)|=1$; let $\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)$ be the length of a shortest reset word, and
$C(n)=\max\{\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A): |Q|=n,\ \mathcal A\text{ synchronizing},\ \Sigma\text{ finite}\}$ (finite, since
$\mathrm{rt}(\mathcal A)<2^n$). Prove $C(n)=o(n^3)$. (Known: $(n-1)^2\le C(n)\le(7/48+15625/798768)\,n^3+o(n^3)
\approx0.1654\,n^3$.)
Formalization notes:
* A complete DFA with `n` states over a `k`-letter alphabet is a transition function
  `δ : Fin n → Fin k → Fin n` (no initial/final states are relevant). Every finite alphabet is
  in bijection with some `Fin k`, so quantifying over all `k : ℕ` covers all finite alphabets.
* The action of a word `w : List (Fin k)` on a state is `List.foldl δ q w` (letters read left
  to right). `w` is a reset word iff all states are sent to the same state, which for `n ≥ 1` is
  `|δ(Q,w)| = 1`.
* `C(n) = o(n³)` is written out: for every `ε > 0` there is `N` such that for all `n ≥ N`,
  every synchronizing `n`-state DFA over any finite alphabet has a reset word of length
  `≤ ε n³`. (Equivalent to `C(n)/n³ → 0`, since `C(n)` is the max of shortest reset lengths.)
* `Claim` = a subcubic bound `C(n) = o(n³)`. `¬Claim` = `C(n) ≥ c n³` for some `c > 0` and
  infinitely many `n` (which would refute the Černý conjecture).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE125
noncomputable section

/-- The state reached from `q` after reading `w`. -/
def run {n k : ℕ} (δ : Fin n → Fin k → Fin n) (q : Fin n) (w : List (Fin k)) : Fin n :=
  w.foldl δ q

/-- `w` is a reset (synchronizing) word: it sends every state to one and the same state. -/
def IsReset {n k : ℕ} (δ : Fin n → Fin k → Fin n) (w : List (Fin k)) : Prop :=
  ∀ q q' : Fin n, run δ q w = run δ q' w

/-- Subcubic reset thresholds: `C(n) = o(n³)`. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → ∀ (k : ℕ) (δ : Fin n → Fin k → Fin n),
    (∃ w : List (Fin k), IsReset δ w) →
      ∃ w : List (Fin k), IsReset δ w ∧ (w.length : ℝ) ≤ ε * (n : ℝ) ^ 3

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE125

title: A regular language of generalized star height two
credit: Classical problem (Eggan 1963 for ordinary star height; generalized version promoted by Brzozowski, Pin, Straubing, Thérien).
premise_risks: The OpenAI <=3 bounds (Sept 2026) are unrefereed; they are context, not premises.
The statement is well known (low novelty) but not on the board.
plain: Regular expressions built from letters using union, concatenation, complement and Kleene star describe exactly the regular languages. The generalized star height of a language is the smallest nesting depth of stars any such expression needs. Languages that need zero stars (the star-free ones) and languages that need one star (like (aa)*) are known, but nobody knows whether any regular language needs two. Decide whether every regular language has generalized star height at most one.
math: Generalized regular expressions over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ are built from $\emptyset,\{\varepsilon\},a\ (a\in\Sigma)$ by $E\cup F$, $EF$, $\Sigma^*\setminus E$ and $E^*$, with height $h(E^*)=1+h(E)$, $h$ of atoms $=0$, and $h$ of the other operations the maximum of the arguments' heights. For regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ let $h_\Sigma(L)=\min\{h(E):\mathcal L(E)=L\}$. Decide whether there exist a finite $\Sigma$ and a regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ with $h_\Sigma(L)\ge2$; equivalently, whether $h_\Sigma(L)\le1$ for every regular $L$. Either answer solves the problem.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E126: A regular language of generalized star height two
Regular expressions built from letters using union, concatenation, complement and Kleene star describe
exactly the regular languages. The generalized star height of a language is the smallest nesting
depth of stars any such expression needs. Languages that need zero stars (the star-free ones) and
languages that need one star (like (aa)*) are known, but nobody knows whether any regular language
needs two. Decide whether every regular language has generalized star height at most one.
Informal statement: Generalized regular expressions over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ are built from
$\emptyset,\{\varepsilon\},a\ (a\in\Sigma)$ by $E\cup F$, $EF$, $\Sigma^*\setminus E$ and $E^*$, with
height $h(E^*)=1+h(E)$, $h$ of atoms $=0$, and $h$ of the other operations the maximum of the
arguments' heights. For regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ let $h_\Sigma(L)=\min\{h(E):\mathcal L(E)=L\}$.
Decide whether there exist a finite $\Sigma$ and a regular $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ with
$h_\Sigma(L)\ge2$; equivalently, whether $h_\Sigma(L)\le1$ for every regular $L$.
Formalization notes:
* `GRE σ` is the inductive type of generalized regular expressions over the alphabet `σ`, with
  the seven constructors above. `GRE.lang` is its semantics in Mathlib's `Language σ`
  (= `Set (List σ)`): `0` is ∅, `1` is {ε}, `+` is union, `*` is concatenation, `ᶜ` is the
  complement in σ* (the Boolean-algebra complement of `Set (List σ)`), and `KStar.kstar` is the
  Kleene star. `GRE.height` is the generalized star height of the expression.
* Regularity is Mathlib's `Language.IsRegular` (accepted by a DFA with finitely many states).
  Every regular language is denoted by an (ordinary, hence generalized) regular expression
  (Kleene), so h_Σ(L) is defined for all regular L.
* The alphabet is `Fin k` for some k; every finite alphabet is in bijection with some `Fin k` and
  relabelling letters preserves heights, so this loses nothing. The height is relative to the
  alphabet (complement is taken in σ*), as in the informal h_Σ.
* `Claim` = there is a regular language of generalized star height ≥ 2 (all expressions denoting
  it have height ≥ 2). `¬Claim` = every regular language over every finite alphabet is denoted by
  an expression of height ≤ 1. Either proof solves the problem.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE126
noncomputable section

/-- Generalized regular expressions (with complement). -/
inductive GRE (σ : Type) : Type
  | zero : GRE σ
  | one : GRE σ
  | sym : σ → GRE σ
  | union : GRE σ → GRE σ → GRE σ
  | concat : GRE σ → GRE σ → GRE σ
  | compl : GRE σ → GRE σ
  | star : GRE σ → GRE σ

namespace GRE

variable {σ : Type}

/-- The language denoted by an expression. -/
def lang : GRE σ → Language σ
  | .zero => 0
  | .one => 1
  | .sym a => {[a]}
  | .union e f => lang e + lang f
  | .concat e f => lang e * lang f
  | .compl e => (lang e)ᶜ
  | .star e => KStar.kstar (lang e)

/-- Generalized star height of an expression. -/
def height : GRE σ → ℕ
  | .zero => 0
  | .one => 0
  | .sym _ => 0
  | .union e f => max (height e) (height f)
  | .concat e f => max (height e) (height f)
  | .compl e => height e
  | .star e => height e + 1

end GRE

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ k : ℕ, ∃ L : Language (Fin k), L.IsRegular ∧
    ∀ e : GRE (Fin k), GRE.lang e = L → 2 ≤ GRE.height e

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE126

title: Two colours, sums of at most two: does every solution compute the halting problem?
credit: Hindman–Leader–Strauss (2003) question; Dzhafarov, Jockusch, Solomon, Westrick; Carlucci, Kołodziejczyk, Lepore, Zdanowski.
premise_risks: The computable formulation is slightly different from the RCA0 implication; a positive answer that relativizes gives HT^{<=2}_2 -> ACA0, a negative answer alone does not separate them.
Check Bompard–Liu–Patey and any 2025-2026 work for an unpublicized resolution.
plain: Hindman's theorem says that for any finite colouring of the positive integers there is an infinite set H all of whose finite sums have one colour. Restrict this to sums of one or two distinct elements. A computable 4-colouring is known to force every such H to compute the halting problem, but with only 2 colours (and no extra 'apartness' condition) nobody knows. Decide whether some computable 2-colouring forces every solution to compute the halting problem.
math: For $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ let $FS^{\le2}(H)=H\cup\{x+y:x,y\in H,\ x\ne y\}$. Decide whether there exists a computable $c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,1\}$ such that every infinite $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ on which $FS^{\le2}(H)$ is $c$-monochromatic satisfies $\emptyset'\le_T H$. Either answer is a solution. (A relativizable positive answer gives $\mathsf{RCA}_0\vdash\mathsf{HT}^{\le2}_2\to\mathsf{ACA}_0$.)

/-! QED-E127: Two colours, sums of at most two: does every solution compute the halting problem?
Hindman's theorem says that for any finite colouring of the positive integers there is an infinite set H all of whose finite sums have one colour. Restrict this to sums of one or two distinct elements. A computable 4-colouring is known to force every such H to compute the halting problem, but with only 2 colours (and no extra 'apartness' condition) nobody knows. Decide whether some computable 2-colouring forces every solution to compute the halting problem.
Informal statement: For $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ let $FS^{\le2}(H)=H\cup\{x+y:x,y\in H,\ x\ne y\}$. Decide whether there exists a computable $c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,1\}$ such that every infinite $H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ on which $FS^{\le2}(H)$ is $c$-monochromatic satisfies $\emptyset'\le_T H$. Either answer is a solution. (A relativizable positive answer gives $\mathsf{RCA}_0\vdash\mathsf{HT}^{\le2}_2\to\mathsf{ACA}_0$.)
Formalization notes:
* Colourings are `c : ℕ → Bool` with Mathlib's `Computable c`; the value `c 0` is irrelevant
  since solutions lie in the positive integers, so this is the same as a computable colouring
  of `ℕ_{>0}`.
* `FS2 H = H ∪ {a + b : a, b ∈ H, a ≠ b}`.
* The halting set `∅'` is `K = {n | φₙ(n)↓}`, where `φₙ` is `Nat.Partrec.Code.eval` of the code
  `Denumerable.ofNat Nat.Partrec.Code n` (Mathlib's standard Gödel numbering of partial
  recursive codes). Sets are represented by their total 0/1 characteristic functions as
  `ℕ →. ℕ` (`Part.some`), and `∅' ≤_T H` is Mathlib's `TuringReducible (chiK) (chi H)`,
  i.e. `chiK` is partial recursive relative to the oracle `chi H` (`RecursiveIn {chi H}`).
* `Claim`: some computable 2-colouring has every infinite monochromatic `FS^{≤2}` solution
  `H ⊆ ℕ_{>0}` computing `∅'`. Solutions exist for every colouring (Hindman), so the
  universal statement is not vacuous. Proving `Claim` or `¬Claim` (every computable 2-colouring
  has an infinite solution not computing `∅'`) both answer the problem.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE127
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Sums of one or two distinct elements of `H`. -/
def FS2 (H : Set ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  {x : ℕ | x ∈ H ∨ ∃ a ∈ H, ∃ b ∈ H, a ≠ b ∧ x = a + b}

/-- Characteristic function of a set, as a total function `ℕ →. ℕ`. -/
def chi (S : Set ℕ) : ℕ →. ℕ := fun n : ℕ => Part.some (if n ∈ S then 1 else 0)

/-- The halting set `∅' = {n | φₙ(n)↓}`. -/
def haltK : Set ℕ :=
  {n : ℕ | (Nat.Partrec.Code.eval (Denumerable.ofNat Nat.Partrec.Code n) n).Dom}

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℕ → Bool, Computable c ∧
    ∀ H : Set ℕ, H.Infinite → (∀ x ∈ H, 0 < x) →
      (∃ b : Bool, ∀ x ∈ FS2 H, c x = b) →
        TuringReducible (chi haltK) (chi H)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE127

title: Only 2^{O(n^2)} triangulated 3-spheres on n vertices?
credit: Gap stated by Kalai (1988), Pfeifle–Ziegler (2004), Nevo–Wilson (2013), Nevo–Santos–Wilson (2016).
premise_risks: Closing this specific log factor is a natural open gap but not singled out as a numbered open problem in the sources; Nevo–Santos–Wilson call their lower bound 'close to' the upper bound.
Durhuus–Pavelka (Nov 2026) is unrefereed; used only for context on the facet version.
plain: Count the triangulations of the 3-dimensional sphere on n labelled vertices. Constructions give at least 2^{cn^2} of them, while the only upper bound, from counting all possible sets of tetrahedra, is 2^{Cn^2 log n}. Decide which is the truth: is the count at most 2^{Cn^2}, or does the log n factor really occur?
math: Let $s(n)$ be the number of simplicial complexes $K$ on vertex set $[n]$ (every vertex used) with $|K|\cong S^3$. Known: $2^{\Omega(n^2)}\le s(n)\le 2^{O(n^2\log n)}$. Decide whether $\log_2 s(n)=O(n^2)$ (i.e. $\exists C\ \forall n:\ s(n)\le 2^{Cn^2}$) or $\log_2 s(n)/n^2\to\infty$ along some subsequence.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-E128: Only 2^{O(n^2)} triangulated 3-spheres on n vertices?
Count the triangulations of the 3-dimensional sphere on n labelled vertices. Constructions give at least 2^{cn^2} of them, while the only upper bound, from counting all possible sets of tetrahedra, is 2^{Cn^2 log n}. Decide which is the truth: is the count at most 2^{Cn^2}, or does the log n factor really occur?
Informal statement: Let $s(n)$ be the number of simplicial complexes $K$ on vertex set $[n]$ (every vertex used) with $|K|\cong S^3$. Known: $2^{\Omega(n^2)}\le s(n)\le 2^{O(n^2\log n)}$. Decide whether $\log_2 s(n)=O(n^2)$ (i.e. $\exists C\ \forall n:\ s(n)\le 2^{Cn^2}$) or $\log_2 s(n)/n^2\to\infty$ along some subsequence.
Formalization notes:
* Complexes. A triangulated 3-sphere is a pure 3-dimensional simplicial complex, determined by
  its set of facets (tetrahedra = 4-element vertex sets); we represent it as
  `Finset (Finset ℕ)` (facets), or `Finset (Finset (Fin n))` for complexes on vertex set [n].
* Which complexes are 3-spheres. We avoid geometric realisations by the following classical
  facts. (1) Every triangulation of a 3-manifold is combinatorial (PL): vertex links are
  triangulated 2-spheres (Moise / standard). (2) Pachner (1991): two closed combinatorial
  manifolds are PL-homeomorphic iff they are related by a finite sequence of bistellar moves and
  a simplicial isomorphism. Hence the complexes K with |K| ≅ S³ are exactly the relabelings of
  complexes reachable from ∂Δ⁴ (the boundary of the 4-simplex on {0,…,4}) by bistellar moves.
* Bistellar move (`Move K K'`): disjoint nonempty A, B with |A| + |B| = 5 such that the facets
  of K containing A are exactly the sets A ∪ (B \ {b}), b ∈ B (i.e. star(A) = A * ∂B), and B is
  not a face of K (not contained in any facet); then replace those facets by B ∪ (A \ {a}),
  a ∈ A (star becomes ∂A * B). The cases |A| = 4, 3, 2, 1 are the 1–4, 2–3, 3–2, 4–1 moves; in the
  1–4 move B = {x} with x a fresh vertex (any unused natural number).
* Relabeling: `IsSphere3 F` iff F is the image of a reachable complex under an injective map
  ℕ → ℕ applied to vertices (this covers simplicial isomorphisms).
* `sphereCount n` (= s(n)) counts facet sets `F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))` that are 3-spheres (after the inclusion
  Fin n → ℕ) and use every vertex of [n]; this is a finite type, counted by `Nat.card`.
  (Counting labelled vs unlabelled, or allowing unused vertices, changes s(n) by at most a factor
  2^{O(n log n)}, irrelevant here.)
* Proving `Claim` = ∃ C, ∀ n, s(n) ≤ 2^{C n²}. Proving `¬Claim` = log₂ s(n)/n² is unbounded, i.e.
  → ∞ along a subsequence (the log n factor genuinely appears, at least partially). This is a
  decision problem: either proof settles it.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE128
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- The boundary of the 4-simplex on `{0,1,2,3,4}`, as its 5 facets. -/
def bdry4Simplex : Finset (Finset ℕ) :=
  (Finset.range 5).image (fun i : ℕ => (Finset.range 5).erase i)

/-- `B` is a face of the complex with facet set `K`. -/
def IsFace (K : Finset (Finset ℕ)) (B : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ F ∈ K, B ⊆ F

/-- Facets of the join `A * ∂B`: the sets `A ∪ (B \ {b})`, `b ∈ B`. -/
def joinBdry (A B : Finset ℕ) : Finset (Finset ℕ) :=
  B.image (fun b : ℕ => A ∪ B.erase b)

/-- A bistellar (Pachner) move on 3-dimensional complexes given by facet sets. -/
def Move (K K' : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ A B : Finset ℕ, A.Nonempty ∧ B.Nonempty ∧ Disjoint A B ∧ A.card + B.card = 5 ∧
    K.filter (fun F : Finset ℕ => A ⊆ F) = joinBdry A B ∧
    ¬ IsFace K B ∧
    K' = (K \ joinBdry A B) ∪ joinBdry B A

/-- `F` (facet set) triangulates the 3-sphere: it is a relabeling of a complex obtained from
`∂Δ⁴` by bistellar moves. -/
def IsSphere3 (F : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ G : Finset (Finset ℕ), Relation.ReflTransGen Move bdry4Simplex G ∧
    ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, Function.Injective f ∧ F = G.image (fun s : Finset ℕ => s.image f)

/-- View a facet set on `Fin n` as one on `ℕ`. -/
def toNat {n : ℕ} (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) : Finset (Finset ℕ) :=
  F.image (fun s : Finset (Fin n) => s.image (fun i : Fin n => (i : ℕ)))

/-- Number of triangulations of `S³` with vertex set exactly `[n] = Fin n`. -/
def sphereCount (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {F : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) //
    IsSphere3 (toNat F) ∧ ∀ i : Fin n, ∃ t ∈ F, i ∈ t}

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, (sphereCount n : ℝ) ≤ (2 : ℝ) ^ (C * (n : ℝ) ^ 2)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE128

title: The centred maximal function diminishes variation
credit: Question raised in the regularity-of-maximal-functions literature (Aldaz-Perez Lazaro; Kurka 2015; Carneiro survey 2019); not a named conjecture.
premise_risks: Continuous/discrete equivalence is proved in 2407.06734 only for the step-function class; state both versions explicitly rather than claiming equivalence in general

plain: Replace a function on the real line by its centred maximal average: at each point take the largest average of |f| over intervals centred there. Discrete companion (also open; a separate statement, not part of the main claim): for finitely supported $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $Mf(n)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb{N}_0}\frac{1}{2r+1}\sum_{|k|\le r}|f(n+k)|$, prove $\sum_{n}|Mf(n+1)-Mf(n)|\le\sum_n|f(n+1)-f(n)|$. The constant 1 cannot be improved.

/-! QED-E129: The centred maximal function diminishes variation
Replace a function on the real line by its centred maximal average: at each point take the largest average of |f| over intervals centred there. The total variation of the new function should be no larger than that of f. This is known for the uncentred maximal function and, for the centred one, for indicator functions and special step functions; for general f the best proven bound allows growth by a factor 240,004.
Informal statement: For locally integrable $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ let
$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{2r}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(y)|\,dy$. Prove or disprove: for every $f$ of bounded variation,
$\operatorname{Var}(Mf)\le\operatorname{Var}(f)$, where $\operatorname{Var}(f)$ is the essential variation (variation
of the best normalized representative) and $\operatorname{Var}(Mf)$ the pointwise variation of the everywhere-defined
function $Mf$. Discrete companion (also open; a separate statement `DiscreteClaim` below, not part of `Claim`): for
finitely supported $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ with
$Mf(n)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb{N}_0}\frac{1}{2r+1}\sum_{|k|\le r}|f(n+k)|$, prove
$\sum_{n}|Mf(n+1)-Mf(n)|\le\sum_n|f(n+1)-f(n)|$. The constant 1 cannot be improved.
Formalization notes:
* `maximalFn f x = sup_{r>0} (2r)⁻¹ ∫_{[x-r,x+r]} |f|`, computed in `ℝ≥0∞` with the lower Lebesgue
  integral (no integrability junk). It depends only on the a.e. class of `f` and is defined at every
  `x`. For `f` of bounded variation, `f` is bounded, so `maximalFn f x ≤ sup |f| < ∞` and taking
  `toReal` loses nothing.
* Variation: Mathlib's `eVariationOn g Set.univ` (supremum over finite increasing sequences of
  `∑ |g(x_{i+1}) - g(x_i)|`, valued in `ℝ≥0∞`), i.e. pointwise variation. For `Mf` this is the
  quantity in the literature (Aldaz–Pérez Lázaro, Kurka): `Mf` is defined everywhere.
* Essential vs pointwise variation of `f`: `Claim` uses the pointwise variation of an arbitrary
  representative `f` with finite variation. This is equivalent to the essential-variation statement:
  pointwise `Var f ≥ essVar f`, so the essential version implies `Claim`; conversely, given `f` with
  finite essential variation, apply `Claim` to its normalized representative `f̃` (pointwise
  `Var f̃ = essVar f`), using `M f = M f̃`. BV functions are differences of monotone functions,
  hence measurable, so "locally integrable" is automatic.
* `Claim` = `Var(Mf) ≤ Var(f)` for all BV `f` on ℝ (continuous, centred). `¬Claim` = an explicit BV
  `f` with `Var(Mf) > Var(f)`.
* `DiscreteClaim` (companion, not part of `Claim`): finitely supported `f : ℤ → ℝ`, discrete centred
  maximal function with radii `r ∈ ℕ` (including `r = 0`, so `Mf ≥ |f|`), sums as `ℝ≥0∞`-valued
  `tsum`s (both sides are finite: the right side is a finite sum, the left side converges since
  `Mf(n) ≍ 1/|n|` has a summable difference sequence; `ℝ≥0∞` avoids junk either way). Equivalence of the
  two versions is known only for special step functions, so they are kept separate.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE129
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Centred Hardy–Littlewood maximal function on ℝ (values in `ℝ≥0∞`). -/
def maximalFn (f : ℝ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (r : ℝ) (_ : 0 < r),
    ENNReal.ofReal (1 / (2 * r)) * ∫⁻ y in Set.Icc (x - r) (x + r), ENNReal.ofReal |f y|

/-- Variation-diminishing property of the centred maximal function on ℝ. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ f : ℝ → ℝ, eVariationOn f Set.univ ≠ ⊤ →
    eVariationOn (fun x : ℝ => (maximalFn f x).toReal) Set.univ ≤ eVariationOn f Set.univ

/-- Discrete centred maximal function on ℤ, radii `r ∈ ℕ` (values in `ℝ≥0∞`). -/
def discMaximalFn (f : ℤ → ℝ) (n : ℤ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ r : ℕ, (∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc (-(r : ℤ)) (r : ℤ), ENNReal.ofReal |f (n + k)|) /
    (2 * (r : ℝ≥0∞) + 1)

/-- Discrete companion (separate open problem, not part of `Claim`). -/
def DiscreteClaim : Prop :=
  ∀ f : ℤ → ℝ, (∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℤ, (N : ℤ) < |n| → f n = 0) →
    ∑' n : ℤ, ENNReal.ofReal |(discMaximalFn f (n + 1)).toReal - (discMaximalFn f n).toReal| ≤
      ∑' n : ℤ, ENNReal.ofReal |f (n + 1) - f n|

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE129

title: Sign uncertainty on the line: reach 1/2
credit: Bourgain-Clozel-Kahane sign uncertainty constant; target 1/2 chosen as first value beyond reach of the 2017 rearrangement method (QED framing).
premise_risks: Threshold 1/2 is a round-number choice, justified only by the 2017 authors' remark that the method yields only third-decimal gains
Upper bound 0.5671 is from an unrefereed AI-search report; refereed upper bound is 0.594
Literature sometimes states the result for A(f)A(f̂) (product) vs its square root; keep the product form 1/4
plain: If a real even function f on the line has f(0) ≤ 0 and its Fourier transform is also ≤ 0 at the origin, then f and its transform cannot both become permanently nonnegative too soon: with A(f), A(f̂) the radii beyond which each is nonnegative, the product A(f)A(f̂) is bounded below. The best proven lower bound for the square root of this product is 0.45 (2017), while the best examples give about 0.567. Prove the bound 1/2.
math: With $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$, let $\mathcal{A}_+$ be the set of nonzero real-valued even continuous $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ with $\hat f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $f(0)\le0$, $\hat f(0)\le0$, and $f,\hat f$ eventually nonnegative; for real $g$ put $A(g)=\inf\{r>0: g(x)\ge0\text{ for all }|x|\ge r\}$. Prove $A(f)A(\hat f)\ge 1/4$ for all $f\in\mathcal{A}_+$, i.e. $\mathbb{A}_+(1):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal A_+}\sqrt{A(f)A(\hat f)}\ge 1/2$ (currently $0.45\le\mathbb{A}_+(1)\le 0.5671$).

/-! QED-E130: Sign uncertainty on the line: reach 1/2
If a real even function f on the line has f(0) ≤ 0 and its Fourier transform is also ≤ 0 at the origin, then f and its transform cannot both become permanently nonnegative too soon: with A(f), A(f̂) the radii beyond which each is nonnegative, the product A(f)A(f̂) is bounded below. The best proven lower bound for the square root of this product is 0.45 (2017), while the best examples give about 0.567. Prove the bound 1/2.
Informal statement: With $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$, let $\mathcal{A}_+$ be the set of nonzero real-valued even continuous $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ with $\hat f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $f(0)\le0$, $\hat f(0)\le0$, and $f,\hat f$ eventually nonnegative; for real $g$ put $A(g)=\inf\{r>0: g(x)\ge0\text{ for all }|x|\ge r\}$. Prove $A(f)A(\hat f)\ge 1/4$ for all $f\in\mathcal{A}_+$, i.e. $\mathbb{A}_+(1):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal A_+}\sqrt{A(f)A(\hat f)}\ge 1/2$ (currently $0.45\le\mathbb{A}_+(1)\le 0.5671$).
Formalization notes:
* Fourier transform with the `e^{-2πixξ}` convention. For even integrable real `f` the sine part
  `∫ f(x) sin(2πxξ) dx` vanishes (odd integrand), so `f̂(ξ) = ∫ f(x) cos(2πxξ) dx` is real; we
  define `fhat` directly as this cosine integral (a Bochner integral over Lebesgue measure).
* Continuity of `f` is added explicitly (the informal statement is sharpened accordingly). This
  is the standard setting (Bourgain–Clozel–Kahane; Gonçalves–Oliveira e Silva–Steinerberger):
  for `f, f̂ ∈ L¹`, `f` agrees a.e. with a continuous function, and the pointwise conditions
  `f(0) ≤ 0` and `A(f)` refer to that representative. Without continuity the statement is
  false for junk reasons: `f = -1` at `0` and `0` elsewhere has `f̂ = 0` and `A(f) = 0`.
* "Nonzero" is `∃ x, f x ≠ 0`, which for continuous `f` means `f ≠ 0` in `L¹`.
* `A g = sInf {r | 0 < r ∧ ∀ x, r ≤ |x| → 0 ≤ g x}`. The eventual-nonnegativity hypotheses make
  this set nonempty, and it is bounded below by 0, so `A g` is the genuine infimum (no junk).
  (`A f = 0` is impossible for admissible `f`: it forces `f ≥ 0` everywhere by continuity, and
  with `∫ f = f̂(0) ≤ 0` this gives `f = 0`.)
* `Claim`: `1/4 ≤ A(f)·A(f̂)` for every admissible `f`, i.e. `𝔸₊(1) ≥ 1/2`. `¬Claim` exhibits an
  admissible `f` with `A(f)A(f̂) < 1/4`, i.e. `𝔸₊(1) < 1/2`.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE130
noncomputable section
open MeasureTheory

/-- Fourier transform of an even real function (`e^{-2πixξ}` convention), which is real. -/
def fhat (f : ℝ → ℝ) (ξ : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x : ℝ, f x * Real.cos (2 * Real.pi * x * ξ)

/-- The radius beyond which `g` is nonnegative. -/
def A (g : ℝ → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  sInf {r : ℝ | 0 < r ∧ ∀ x : ℝ, r ≤ |x| → 0 ≤ g x}

/-- The class `𝒜₊` of the `+1` sign uncertainty principle on `ℝ`. -/
def Admissible (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  Continuous f ∧ Integrable f ∧ Integrable (fhat f) ∧ (∀ x : ℝ, f (-x) = f x) ∧
    (∃ x : ℝ, f x ≠ 0) ∧ f 0 ≤ 0 ∧ fhat f 0 ≤ 0 ∧
    (∃ R : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, R ≤ |x| → 0 ≤ f x) ∧
    (∃ R : ℝ, ∀ ξ : ℝ, R ≤ |ξ| → 0 ≤ fhat f ξ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ f : ℝ → ℝ, Admissible f → (1 : ℝ) / 4 ≤ A f * A (fhat f)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE130

title: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 4
credit: Classical; Conway–Sloane
premise_risks: Unrefereed 2026 claimed proofs (preprints.org 202606.0856; arXiv:2609.25120) — verify status
plain: What is the densest way to pack equal balls in 4-dimensional space? The D4 lattice packing (density π²/16) is believed optimal and has been known to be the best lattice packing since 1873, but denser non-lattice packings have never been ruled out. Prove that no packing beats π²/16.
math: Let $\Delta_4$ be the supremum, over all packings of congruent open balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, of the upper density $\limsup_{R\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(\bigcup B\cap B(0,R))/\mathrm{vol}(B(0,R))$. Prove $\Delta_4=\pi^2/16$, the density of the $D_4$ lattice packing.

/-! QED-E131: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 4
What is the densest way to pack equal balls in 4-dimensional space? The D4 lattice packing (density π²/16) is believed optimal and has been known to be the best lattice packing since 1873, but denser non-lattice packings have never been ruled out. Prove that no packing beats π²/16.
Informal statement: Let $\Delta_4$ be the supremum, over all packings of congruent open balls in $\mathbb{R}^4$, of the upper density $\limsup_{R\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(\bigcup B\cap B(0,R))/\mathrm{vol}(B(0,R))$. Prove $\Delta_4=\pi^2/16$, the density of the $D_4$ lattice packing.
Formalization notes:
* Space: `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 4)` with its `volume` (Lebesgue measure) and Euclidean metric,
  as in QED-E040 (heptagon packing), whose density definitions are reused here.
* Packing: a set `S` of centres with pairwise distances ≥ 2; the packing is the union of the
  open unit balls `ball x 1`, x ∈ S, which are pairwise disjoint exactly when distinct centres are
  at distance ≥ 2. Density is invariant under scaling, so radius 1 is no loss. `S` may be finite
  (density 0) or infinite (it is automatically countable).
* Density: upper density = limsup over R → ∞ of vol(⋃ balls ∩ B(0,R)) / vol(B(0,R)) in `ℝ≥0∞`
  (no junk values: numerator ≤ denominator < ∞, denominator > 0 for R > 0). Δ₄ = supremum over
  packings. The informal source used cubes [-R,R]⁴ instead of balls B(0,R); the supremum over
  packings is the same for either exhaustion (standard; cf. Rogers, Conway–Sloane), and balls are
  used for consistency with QED-E040. Open vs closed balls does not change volumes.
* The D₄ packing (centres the vectors of √2·D₄, minimal distance 2) has density π²/16, so
  Δ₄ ≥ π²/16 is known; the open content is Δ₄ ≤ π²/16. Proving `Claim` = Δ₄ = π²/16 (D₄ is an
  optimal packing). Proving `¬Claim` = Δ₄ ≠ π²/16, i.e. some packing has upper density > π²/16.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE131
noncomputable section
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Ambient Euclidean space `ℝ⁴`. -/
abbrev E : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 4)

/-- A packing of unit balls: centres pairwise at distance at least 2. -/
def IsPacking (S : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ y ∈ S, x ≠ y → (2 : ℝ) ≤ dist x y

/-- Fraction of the ball of radius `R` about the origin covered by the open unit balls centred
at the points of `S`. -/
def coveredFraction (S : Set E) (R : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  MeasureTheory.volume ((⋃ x ∈ S, Metric.ball x 1) ∩ Metric.ball (0 : E) R) /
    MeasureTheory.volume (Metric.ball (0 : E) R)

/-- Upper density of a packing: `limsup_{R → ∞}` of the covered fraction. -/
def upperDensity (S : Set E) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  Filter.limsup (fun R : ℝ => coveredFraction S R) Filter.atTop

/-- The sphere packing density `Δ₄` of `ℝ⁴`. -/
def packingDensity : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (S : Set E) (_ : IsPacking S), upperDensity S

def Claim : Prop := packingDensity = ENNReal.ofReal (Real.pi ^ 2 / 16)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE131

title: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 5, 6 or 7
credit: Classical
plain: In dimensions 5, 6 and 7 the densest known ball packings come from the lattices D5, E6 and E7, which are known to be the best lattice packings. Prove that at least one of them is optimal among all packings.
math: Let $\Delta_n$ be the supremum of upper densities of packings of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Prove that at least one of $\Delta_5=\pi^2/(15\sqrt2)$ (density of $D_5$), $\Delta_6=\pi^3/(48\sqrt3)$ (density of $E_6$), $\Delta_7=\pi^3/105$ (density of $E_7$) holds.

/-! QED-E132: Optimal sphere packing in dimension 5, 6 or 7
In dimensions 5, 6 and 7 the densest known ball packings come from the lattices D5, E6 and E7, which are known to be the best lattice packings. Prove that at least one of them is optimal among all packings.
Informal statement: Let $\Delta_n$ be the supremum of upper densities of packings of congruent balls in
$\mathbb{R}^n$. Prove that at least one of $\Delta_5=\pi^2/(15\sqrt2)$ (density of $D_5$),
$\Delta_6=\pi^3/(48\sqrt3)$ (density of $E_6$), $\Delta_7=\pi^3/105$ (density of $E_7$) holds.
Formalization notes:
* Same packing-density definition as the board's convex-body packing problems (QED-E040),
  parametrised by the dimension: space `E n = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` with `volume`; a packing
  of congruent copies of `K` is a sequence `g : ℕ → E n ≃ᵢ E n` of isometries with pairwise
  disjoint interiors `interior (g i '' K)`; upper density = `limsup_{R→∞}` of
  `vol(⋃ copies ∩ B(0,R)) / vol(B(0,R))` in `ℝ≥0∞`; `packingDensity n K` = supremum over packings.
  Indexing by ℕ loses nothing (packings of a body with nonempty interior are countable; finite
  packings have density 0), and limsup about the origin gives the standard supremum (Rogers).
* Balls: `K = closedBall 0 1` (density is scale invariant). Isometric images of a ball are balls
  of radius 1, and interiors are open balls, so a packing is exactly a set of unit balls with
  centres at mutual distance ≥ 2. `Δ n := packingDensity n (closedBall 0 1)`.
* Constants: centre density of D₅, E₆, E₇ times the unit-ball volume gives
  `π²/(15√2) ≈ 0.4653`, `π³/(48√3) ≈ 0.3729`, `π³/105 ≈ 0.2953`. The lattice packings give
  `Δ n ≥` these values, so each equality is equivalent to optimality of the lattice packing among
  all packings.
* `Claim` = the disjunction (at least one of the three dimensions is solved by its lattice).
  `¬Claim` = in each of dimensions 5, 6, 7 some packing has upper density strictly exceeding the
  lattice value.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE132
noncomputable section
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Ambient Euclidean space of dimension `n`. -/
abbrev E (n : ℕ) : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)

/-- A packing of congruent copies of `K`: a sequence of isometries of `E n` whose images of `K`
have pairwise disjoint interiors. -/
def IsPacking {n : ℕ} (K : Set (E n)) (g : ℕ → (E n ≃ᵢ E n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≠ j → Disjoint (interior (g i '' K)) (interior (g j '' K))

/-- Fraction of the ball of radius `R` about the origin covered by the packing. -/
def coveredFraction {n : ℕ} (K : Set (E n)) (g : ℕ → (E n ≃ᵢ E n)) (R : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  MeasureTheory.volume ((⋃ i : ℕ, g i '' K) ∩ Metric.ball (0 : E n) R) /
    MeasureTheory.volume (Metric.ball (0 : E n) R)

/-- Upper density of a packing: `limsup_{R → ∞}` of the covered fraction. -/
def upperDensity {n : ℕ} (K : Set (E n)) (g : ℕ → (E n ≃ᵢ E n)) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  Filter.limsup (fun R : ℝ => coveredFraction K g R) Filter.atTop

/-- Maximal packing density of congruent copies of `K` in `E n`. -/
def packingDensity (n : ℕ) (K : Set (E n)) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (g : ℕ → (E n ≃ᵢ E n)) (_ : IsPacking K g), upperDensity K g

/-- The sphere-packing constant `Δ_n`. -/
def spherePackingDensity (n : ℕ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  packingDensity n (Metric.closedBall (0 : E n) 1)

/-- At least one of the lattices D₅, E₆, E₇ is an optimal sphere packing. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  spherePackingDensity 5 = ENNReal.ofReal (Real.pi ^ 2 / (15 * Real.sqrt 2)) ∨
  spherePackingDensity 6 = ENNReal.ofReal (Real.pi ^ 3 / (48 * Real.sqrt 3)) ∨
  spherePackingDensity 7 = ENNReal.ofReal (Real.pi ^ 3 / 105)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE132

title: Beat (3+√2)/2 for diamond-free families
credit: Problem line from Griggs–Lu and Griggs–Li–Lu. Upper bound (3+√2)/2 by Grósz, Methuku, Tompkins (2018). Lower bound 2.1479 by Tompkins (2026). Three-layer bound by Balogh, Hu, Lidický, Liu.
premise_risks: The lower bound 2.1479 (and the disproof of the diamond conjecture) rests on an unrefereed July 2026 preprint (arXiv:2607.09497). The Claim itself does not depend on it.
The Ai–Liu–Song window-density results are an unrefereed 2026 preprint.
An improved upper bound might exist in a recent preprint not indexed by search.
plain: A family of subsets of {1,...,n} is diamond-free if it contains no four distinct sets A, B, C, D with A ⊂ B ⊂ D and A ⊂ C ⊂ D. For years it was believed that the two middle layers, about 2·binom(n, n/2) sets, are optimal; in July 2026 a random linear-algebra construction beat that with about 2.1479·binom(n, n/2) sets. The best general upper bound, (3+√2)/2 ≈ 2.2071 times binom(n, n/2), dates from 2016–2018. Lower it by any fixed amount.
math: Let $La(n,Q_2)$ be the maximum size of $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ containing no four distinct $A,B,C,D\in\mathcal F$ with $A\subsetneq B\subsetneq D$ and $A\subsetneq C\subsetneq D$. Prove that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} La(n,Q_2)/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} < \frac{3+\sqrt2}{2}$. (Known: $\liminf \ge 2+\frac{29}{135}\prod_{i\ge1}(1-4^{-i})\approx 2.1479$; for families inside three consecutive middle layers the density is at most $2.15121$. Stretch goal: determine the limit, whose existence is itself unknown.)

/-! QED-E133: Beat (3+√2)/2 for diamond-free families
A family of subsets of {1,...,n} is diamond-free if it contains no four distinct sets A, B, C, D with A ⊂ B ⊂ D and A ⊂ C ⊂ D. For years it was believed that the two middle layers, about 2·binom(n, n/2) sets, are optimal; in July 2026 a random linear-algebra construction beat that with about 2.1479·binom(n, n/2) sets. The best general upper bound, (3+√2)/2 ≈ 2.2071 times binom(n, n/2), dates from 2016–2018. Lower it by any fixed amount.
Informal statement: Let $La(n,Q_2)$ be the maximum size of $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ containing no four distinct $A,B,C,D\in\mathcal F$ with $A\subsetneq B\subsetneq D$ and $A\subsetneq C\subsetneq D$. Prove that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} La(n,Q_2)/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} < \frac{3+\sqrt2}{2}$. (Known: $\liminf \ge 2+\frac{29}{135}\prod_{i\ge1}(1-4^{-i})\approx 2.1479$; for families inside three consecutive middle layers the density is at most $2.15121$. Stretch goal: determine the limit, whose existence is itself unknown.)
Formalization notes:
* A family is a `Finset (Finset (Fin n))` (ground set [n] = Fin n). `DiamondFree F` forbids A, B, C, D ∈ F with
  A ⊂ B ⊂ D, A ⊂ C ⊂ D (strict inclusions) and B ≠ C. Strictness makes A, B, D and A, C, D pairwise distinct, and
  B ≠ C completes distinctness, so this is exactly the non-induced (weak) Q₂-free condition used for La(n, Q₂)
  (B, C may be comparable).
* `La n` is the maximum of `F.card` over diamond-free families (a `Finset.sup` over the finite type of all families;
  the empty family is diamond-free, so the max is genuine).
* For a real sequence a, limsup a < L ⇔ ∃ c < L with a n ≤ c eventually. `Claim` states the right-hand side with
  a n = La n / C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) and L = (3+√2)/2, avoiding a junk-valued limsup. Proving `Claim` = lowering the
  (3+√2)/2 upper bound by a fixed amount; ¬Claim = limsup La(n,Q₂)/C(n,⌊n/2⌋) ≥ (3+√2)/2 (given the known upper
  bound, equal to it).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE133
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- No A ⊂ B ⊂ D, A ⊂ C ⊂ D in `F` with B ≠ C (a weak copy of the diamond poset Q₂). -/
def DiamondFree {n : ℕ} (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ A ∈ F, ∃ B ∈ F, ∃ C ∈ F, ∃ D ∈ F, A ⊂ B ∧ B ⊂ D ∧ A ⊂ C ∧ C ⊂ D ∧ B ≠ C

/-- La(n, Q₂): the largest size of a diamond-free family of subsets of [n]. -/
def La (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Finset (Fin n)))).filter
    (fun F : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) => DiamondFree F)).sup Finset.card

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, c < (3 + Real.sqrt 2) / 2 ∧
    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, (La n : ℝ) ≤ c * (Nat.choose n (n / 2) : ℝ)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE133

title: Turán density of the tight 5-cycle
credit: Conjectured value from the Mubayi–Rödl construction (the conjecture is usually attributed to them, but the problem is not person-named). Upper bound by Razborov. Related progress by Kamčev, Letzter, Pokrovskiy and the authors of arXiv:2506.03223.
premise_risks: The conjecture is sometimes informally attributed to Mubayi and Rödl, which is a mild naming risk. It is normally stated simply as 'π(C_5^3) = 2√3 − 3'.
The best upper bound might have been sharpened slightly by unpublished flag-algebra runs (for example 0.4683 vs 0.468). This does not affect the target.
plain: A 3-uniform hypergraph is a collection of triples of points. The tight 5-cycle consists of five points v0,...,v4 arranged in a circle together with the five triples of cyclically consecutive points. What is the largest fraction of all triples a hypergraph on n points can contain without a tight 5-cycle, as n grows?   ∃ k : ℕ, ∃ xs : ℕ → ℚ, ∃ ns : ℕ → ℕ, xs 0 = x ∧

  ∀ x : ℚ, 0 < x → x < 1 → Odd x.den → Terminates x

end OpenProblems.QEDE139

math: Decide whether there exists a finite incidence structure with $157$ points and $157$ lines in which every line contains exactly $13$ points, every point lies on exactly $13$ lines, and any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line. Equivalently: is there a $157\times157$ $0/1$ matrix $A$ with $AA^{\mathsf T}=12I+J$, or equivalently are there $11$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $12$?

/-! QED-E143: Does a projective plane of order 12 exist?
A finite projective plane of order n has n^2+n+1 points and the same number of lines. Every line has n+1 points, and any two points lie on exactly one common line. Planes exist whenever n is a prime power, they are impossible for n = 6 and n = 10, and no plane is known for any other n. The smallest unsettled order is 12.
Informal statement: Decide whether there exists a finite incidence structure with $157$ points and $157$ lines in which every line contains exactly $13$ points, every point lies on exactly $13$ lines, and any two distinct points lie on exactly one common line. Equivalently: is there a $157\times157$ $0/1$ matrix $A$ with $AA^{\mathsf T}=12I+J$, or equivalently are there $11$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $12$?
Formalization notes:
* Points are Fin 157; lines are 13-element subsets of the points, collected in a Finset B (so lines are distinct as
  point sets, as in a projective plane). `Claim`: |B| = 157, every line has 13 points, and any two distinct points
  lie on exactly one line of B.
* This is exactly a projective plane of order 12: a 2-(157,13,1) design. Counting gives each point on
  156/12 = 13 lines and |B| = 157·156/(13·12) = 157 (so the |B| condition is redundant but stated for fidelity), and
  two distinct lines meet in exactly one point (Fisher/symmetric-design argument); non-degeneracy is automatic.
  Conversely a projective plane of order 12 gives such B.
* Decision problem: proving `Claim` = constructing a projective plane of order 12; ¬Claim = none exists.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE143

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Finset (Finset (Fin 157)), B.card = 157 ∧ (∀ b ∈ B, b.card = 13) ∧
    ∀ x y : Fin 157, x ≠ y → ∃! b : Finset (Fin 157), b ∈ B ∧ x ∈ b ∧ y ∈ b

end OpenProblems.QEDE143

end

    (∀ s : Finset (Fin 8), s.card = 3 → ¬ Collinear ℝ (p '' (s : Set (Fin 8)))) ∧

/-! QED-E147: How many faces can a convex space-filler have?
A convex polyhedron is a space-filler if congruent copies of it fill all of 3-space with no gaps or overlaps. In the plane a convex tile has at most 6 sides, but in space the record is 38 faces (Engel, 1981). Is there any finite upper bound at all on the number of faces of a convex space-filler?
Informal statement: Call a convex polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with nonempty interior a monohedral prototile if there are isometries $g_1,g_2,\dots$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\bigcup_i g_iP=\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\operatorname{int}(g_iP)\cap\operatorname{int}(g_jP)=\emptyset$ for $i\neq j$ (the tiling need not be face-to-face, isohedral or periodic). Decide whether there is $N<\infty$ such that every monohedral prototile in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has at most $N$ facets.
Formalization notes:
* E = `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)` (Euclidean metric). A convex polytope is the convex hull of
  a finite point set `S`; we require nonempty interior (3-dimensional).
* Tiling: a sequence `g : ℕ → E ≃ᵢ E` of isometries (orientation-reversing ones allowed, the
  standard meaning of "congruent copies") whose images cover E and have pairwise disjoint
  interiors. Indexing by ℕ loses nothing: tiles with disjoint nonempty interiors are at most
  countably many, and finitely many compact tiles cannot cover E.
* Facets: F is a facet of P if F = {x ∈ P | ⟪a,x⟫ = sup_P ⟪a,·⟫} for some a ≠ 0 (an exposed
  face; P is compact and nonempty so the sSup is a genuine maximum) and the affine span of F
  has dimension 2. For a 3-polytope these are exactly its 2-dimensional faces.
* To avoid the junk value of cardinalities of possibly infinite sets, "P has at most N facets"
  is stated as: every finite family of distinct facets has at most N members.
* `Claim` = there is a uniform bound N. `¬Claim` = convex space-fillers with arbitrarily
  many facets exist.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE147
noncomputable section
open scoped InnerProductSpace RealInnerProductSpace

abbrev E := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- `P` tiles space by congruent copies. -/
def Tiles (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∃ g : ℕ → (E ≃ᵢ E),
    (⋃ i : ℕ, (g i) '' P) = Set.univ ∧
    ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≠ j → Disjoint (interior ((g i) '' P)) (interior ((g j) '' P))

/-- `F` is a facet (2-dimensional exposed face) of `P`. -/
def IsFacet (P F : Set E) : Prop :=
  (∃ a : E, a ≠ 0 ∧
    F = {x : E | x ∈ P ∧ ⟪a, x⟫_ℝ = sSup ((fun y : E => ⟪a, y⟫_ℝ) '' P)}) ∧
  Module.finrank ℝ (affineSpan ℝ F).direction = 2

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ S : Finset E,
    (interior (convexHull ℝ (S : Set E))).Nonempty →
    Tiles (convexHull ℝ (S : Set E)) →
    ∀ 𝓕 : Finset (Set E), (∀ F ∈ 𝓕, IsFacet (convexHull ℝ (S : Set E)) F) → 𝓕.card ≤ N

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE147

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE148
noncomputable section

/-- Embed an integer point of ℤ⁴ into ℝ⁴. -/
def toR (z : Fin 4 → ℤ) : Fin 4 → ℝ := fun i : Fin 4 => (z i : ℝ)

/-- The lattice polytope with vertex set (contained in) `V`. -/
def poly (V : Finset (Fin 4 → ℤ)) : Set (Fin 4 → ℝ) :=
  convexHull ℝ (toR '' (V : Set (Fin 4 → ℤ)))

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ V : Finset (Fin 4 → ℤ),
    Set.ncard {z : Fin 4 → ℤ | toR z ∈ interior (poly V)} = 1 →
      MeasureTheory.volume (poly V) ≤ (147 : ENNReal)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE148

/-! QED-E149: Every centrally symmetric 5-polytope has at least 243 faces
A polytope is centrally symmetric if it looks the same after reflection through its centre, like a cube or an octahedron. The 5-dimensional cube has 3^5 = 243 non-empty faces (counting the polytope itself), and so does the 5-dimensional cross-polytope. It is conjectured that no centrally symmetric 5-polytope has fewer. Formalization notes:
* ℝ⁵ is Fin 5 → ℝ (product topology = Euclidean) with the standard dot product `dot a x = ∑ a i * x i`.
  A polytope is P = convexHull of a finite set V; full-dimensional: interior P nonempty; centrally symmetric:
  x ∈ P → −x ∈ P (equivalently P = −P).
* `IsFace P F`: F = {x ∈ P | ∀ y ∈ P, dot a y ≤ dot a x} for some a (the maximizers of a linear functional; a = 0
  gives P). These are exactly the nonempty faces of P (P is compact and nonempty, so each such set is nonempty;
  the empty face is not counted).
* "At least 243 faces" is stated as an injection Fin 243 → faces, avoiding `ncard` junk values (faces of a polytope
  are finitely many, but the injection form needs no finiteness argument).
* Proving `Claim` = the 3^d conjecture in dimension 5; ¬Claim = a centrally symmetric 5-polytope with < 243
  nonempty faces.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE149
noncomputable section

def dot (a x : Fin 5 → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ i : Fin 5, a i * x i

/-- F is a nonempty face of P: the set of maximizers in P of some linear functional. -/
def IsFace (P F : Set (Fin 5 → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ a : Fin 5 → ℝ, F = {x : Fin 5 → ℝ | x ∈ P ∧ ∀ y ∈ P, dot a y ≤ dot a x}

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ V : Finset (Fin 5 → ℝ),
    (interior (convexHull ℝ (V : Set (Fin 5 → ℝ)))).Nonempty →
    (∀ x ∈ convexHull ℝ (V : Set (Fin 5 → ℝ)), -x ∈ convexHull ℝ (V : Set (Fin 5 → ℝ))) →
    ∃ F : Fin 243 → Set (Fin 5 → ℝ), Function.Injective F ∧
      ∀ i : Fin 243, IsFace (convexHull ℝ (V : Set (Fin 5 → ℝ))) (F i)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE149

/-! QED-E150: Beat n^2 empty triangles
Scatter n points in the plane with no three on a line. A triangle with corners among the points is empty if no other point is inside it. Every such configuration has at least about n^2 empty triangles, and the best constructions have about 1.62 n^2. Show that every configuration actually has at least (1+c) n^2 empty triangles for some fixed c > 0.
Informal statement: For a finite $S\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three points collinear, let $e(S)$ be the number of 3-subsets $T\subseteq S$ with $\operatorname{conv}(T)\cap S=T$. Let $h_3(n)=\min_{|S|=n}e(S)$. Prove that there is $c>0$ with $h_3(n)\ge(1+c)\,n^2$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
Formalization notes:
* The plane is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`; a point set is a `Finset` of it.
* General position: every 3-element subset is not `Collinear ℝ`.
* `emptyTri S` = 3-subsets T of S (via `powersetCard 3`) such that every point of S lying in the
  closed convex hull of T is a vertex of T, i.e. conv(T) ∩ S = T. In general position no other
  point can lie on an edge, so closed vs open hull does not matter.
* "h₃(n) ≥ (1+c)n² for large n" is stated as a bound for every general-position S with
  |S| ≥ N, which is equivalent because h₃(n) is the minimum of e(S) over |S| = n.
* Claim: ∃ c > 0, ∃ N, all such S with N ≤ |S| have (1+c)|S|² ≤ e(S). ¬Claim: liminf h₃(n)/n² ≤ 1
  (so, with the known lower bound, h₃(n) = (1+o(1))n² along a subsequence).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE150
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

abbrev Plane := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)

def GeneralPosition (S : Finset Plane) : Prop :=
  ∀ T : Finset Plane, T ⊆ S → T.card = 3 → ¬ Collinear ℝ (T : Set Plane)

/-- The empty triangles of `S`: 3-subsets whose convex hull meets `S` only in their vertices. -/
def emptyTri (S : Finset Plane) : Finset (Finset Plane) :=

title: Does the classical Hénon map have a periodic sink?
credit: Hénon (1976); open question as framed by Galias & Tucker (2015)
premise_risks: A positive answer could come from a pure computer search (a certified long-period sink). That is a legitimate solution, but some reviewers may see it as computational.
A negative answer is far beyond current techniques, so the problem may sit open for a long time either way.
plain: The Hénon map H(x,y) = (1 − 1.4x² + y, 0.3x) is the textbook example of a 'strange attractor': on a computer screen its orbits trace out a fractal set. No one has proved that what we see is not just a stable periodic orbit with a very long period. Decide whether H has an attracting periodic orbit.
math: Let $H(x,y)=(1-\tfrac{7}{5}x^2+y,\ \tfrac{3}{10}x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Decide whether there exist $n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $H^n(p)=p$ such that both eigenvalues of $DH^n(p)$ have modulus $<1$.

/-! QED-E152: Does the classical Hénon map have a periodic sink?
The Hénon map H(x,y) = (1 − 1.4x² + y, 0.3x) is the textbook example of a 'strange attractor': on a computer screen its orbits trace out a fractal set. No one has proved that what we see is not just a stable periodic orbit with a very long period. Decide whether H has an attracting periodic orbit.
Informal statement: Let $H(x,y)=(1-\tfrac{7}{5}x^2+y,\ \tfrac{3}{10}x)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Decide whether there exist $n\ge1$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $H^n(p)=p$ such that both eigenvalues of $DH^n(p)$ have modulus $<1$.
Formalization notes:
* H is defined exactly (7/5 = 1.4, 3/10 = 0.3). Its Jacobian at (x, y) is `J (x, y) = !![-(14/5) x, 1; 3/10, 0]`.
  By the chain rule DHⁿ(p) = J(H^{n−1} p) ⋯ J(H p) J(p); `jac n p` is this product, defined recursively
  (jac 0 p = 1, jac (k+1) p = J(H^[k] p) * jac k p), so no fderiv API is needed.
* The eigenvalues of a real 2×2 matrix M are the complex roots of z² − tr(M) z + det(M); trace and determinant are
  written out from the entries. "Both eigenvalues have modulus < 1" is stated as: every complex root z of this
  polynomial has ‖z‖ < 1.
* `Claim`: there exist n ≥ 1 and p with Hⁿ(p) = p whose eigenvalues of DHⁿ(p) lie in the open unit disk, i.e. H has
  an attracting periodic orbit (a sink). Decision problem: proving `Claim` = exhibit a sink (e.g. certified
  computation); ¬Claim = H has no periodic sink.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDE152
noncomputable section

/-- The classical Hénon map. -/
def H (p : ℝ × ℝ) : ℝ × ℝ := (1 - 7 / 5 * p.1 ^ 2 + p.2, 3 / 10 * p.1)

/-- Jacobian matrix of H at p. -/
def J (p : ℝ × ℝ) : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℝ := !![-(14 / 5) * p.1, 1; 3 / 10, 0]

/-- Jacobian matrix of H^[n] at p, by the chain rule. -/
def jac : ℕ → ℝ × ℝ → Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℝ
  | 0, _ => 1
  | k + 1, p => J (H^[k] p) * jac k p

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n ∧ ∃ p : ℝ × ℝ, H^[n] p = p ∧
    ∀ z : ℂ, z ^ 2 - (((jac n p) 0 0 + (jac n p) 1 1 : ℝ) : ℂ) * z
        + (((jac n p) 0 0 * (jac n p) 1 1 - (jac n p) 0 1 * (jac n p) 1 0 : ℝ) : ℂ) = 0 → ‖z‖ < 1

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE152

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE153
noncomputable section

def mandelbrot : Set ℂ :=

def Claim : Prop :=
  MeasureTheory.volume (frontier mandelbrot) = 0

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE153

namespace OpenProblems.QEDE155
noncomputable section

/-- H_n − log n. -/
def gammaSeq (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ k ∈ Finset.range n, (1 : ℝ) / ((k : ℝ) + 1)) - Real.log (n : ℝ)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ g : ℝ, Filter.Tendsto gammaSeq Filter.atTop (nhds g) → Irrational g

end
end OpenProblems.QEDE155

title: Can additive squares be avoided over the integers?
credit: T. C. Brown and A. R. Freedman (1987); G. Pirillo and S. Varricchio (1994); see also Halbeisen-Hungerbühler, Cassaigne-Currie-Schaeffer-Shallit.

plain: An additive square in a sequence of integers is a block of 2k consecutive terms whose first half and second half have the same sum (for example 1 3 | 2 2). Is there a finite set of integers S and an infinite sequence with all terms in S that contains no additive square? Such sequences exist over a finite subset of the plane lattice Z², and over Z one can avoid additive cubes (three adjacent blocks of equal length and equal sum), but no one knows whether squares can be avoided over Z.

Equivalently, by compactness: is there a finite $S\subset\mathbb Z$ for which arbitrarily long finite words over $S$ avoid additive squares?

Such sequences exist over a finite subset of the plane lattice Z², and over Z one can avoid additive cubes (three adjacent blocks of equal length and equal sum), but no one knows whether squares can be avoided over Z.

def AddSqFree (w : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Finset ℤ, ∃ w : ℕ → ℤ, (∀ n : ℕ, w n ∈ S) ∧ AddSqFree w

title: Square-free words from lists of size three

plain: Thue showed in 1906 that there is an infinite word over three letters with no square, that is, no block immediately repeated (like 'abab'). Now suppose each position i has its own list A_i of three allowed symbols, chosen by an adversary from an unbounded alphabet. Is there always an infinite square-free word whose i-th letter lies in A_i? Lists of size 4 are known to suffice, and size 3 suffices when all lists are drawn from only four symbols.

(By compactness, this is equivalent to the same statement for every finite length; that is, the Thue choice number of the path is $3$.)

Thue showed in 1906 that there is an infinite word over three letters with no square, that is, no block immediately repeated (like 'abab'). Now suppose each position i has its own list A_i of three allowed symbols, chosen by an adversary from an unbounded alphabet. Is there always an infinite square-free word whose i-th letter lies in A_i? Lists of size 4 are known to suffice, and size 3 suffices when all lists are drawn from only four symbols.

def SquareFree (w : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i k : ℕ, 0 < k → ∃ j : ℕ, j < k ∧ w (i + j) ≠ w (i + k + j)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ A : ℕ → Finset ℕ, (∀ i : ℕ, (A i).card = 3) →
    ∃ w : ℕ → ℕ, (∀ i : ℕ, w i ∈ A i) ∧ SquareFree w

end
